title: Nature Restoration Academy 2026 in Berlin: Apply for Free Marine and Freshwater Restoration Training
summary: Applications are now open for the Nature Restoration Academy 2026, a free training initiative designed to develop practical skills in marine and freshwater ecosystem restoration. Organized and hosted by the SUBMARINER Network for Blue Growth, the programme combines an online introductory session with an intensive two-day, in-person training event at the organization’s office in Berlin, Germany. Selected participants will learn through expert lectures, practical workshops, European restoration case studies, digital monitoring approaches, and a multi-stakeholder negotiation simulation. The programme is intended to help the next generation of restoration professionals translate environmental research and scientific knowledge into practical action. It will address the recovery of rivers, lakes, wetlands, coastal ecosystems, seas, and connected aquatic environments across the land–freshwater–marine continuum. Participation is free, but only 30 places are available. Applicants must submit their applications by September 15, 2026. Selected participants will be notified by October 1, 2026. Full details are available in the official SUBMARINER Network announcement . Nature Restoration Academy 2026: Key Information Programme information Details Programme name Nature Restoration Academy Main subject Marine and freshwater ecosystem restoration Host organization SUBMARINER Network for Blue Growth Funding organization EIT Water Supporting organization Poul Due Jensen Foundation, also known as the Grundfos Foundation Online baseline session October 6, 2026 In-person training dates October 29–30, 2026 Location SUBMARINER Network office, Berlin, Germany Duration One online session followed by two days of in-person training Participation fee Free of charge Available places Maximum of 30 participants Travel assistance A contribution may be available for participants travelling from outside Germany Application deadline September 15, 2026 Selection notification By October 1, 2026 Application requirement Motivation statement and short CV Application form Nature Restoration Academy Application Form What Is the Nature Restoration Academy? The Nature Restoration Academy is a new capacity-building initiative focused on practical methods for restoring marine and freshwater ecosystems. The programme responds to the growing need for people who can connect environmental science, public policy, community participation, monitoring systems, and sustainable finance with real restoration projects. Its purpose is not limited to explaining restoration concepts theoretically. Instead, the Academy aims to develop practical understanding that participants can apply in their studies, employment, research, policy work, conservation programmes, or community initiatives. The Academy covers ecosystems as an interconnected continuum. This means restoration is not treated as a series of isolated activities. Rivers, lakes, wetlands, estuaries, coasts, and marine environments are considered connected systems in which changes in one area may affect conditions elsewhere. For example, freshwater quality can influence coastal ecosystems, while wetland degradation may affect biodiversity, water storage, flood management, nutrient flows, and surrounding communities. An integrated restoration approach therefore requires coordination across scientific disciplines, geographic boundaries, institutions, and stakeholder groups. The programme has been designed to help participants understand these relationships and convert restoration knowledge into implementable solutions. Who Organizes the Nature Restoration Academy? The Academy is organized and hosted by the SUBMARINER Network for Blue Growth. The SUBMARINER Network is a cooperation platform that connects research and educational institutions, public authorities, civil society organizations, business support institutions, and private companies working within the sustainable blue economy. Although the network is rooted in the Baltic Sea Region, its partnerships and activities extend across Europe and beyond. Its work includes marine conservation, protected areas, sustainable aquaculture, blue biotechnology, maritime spatial planning, ecosystem restoration, policy development, innovation, and capacity-building. The Nature Restoration Academy is funded by EIT Water and supported by the Poul Due Jensen Foundation, also known as the Grundfos Foundation. Why Marine and Freshwater Restoration Training Matters Aquatic ecosystems provide essential environmental, social, and economic services. Healthy rivers, lakes, wetlands, coastal areas, and seas can support biodiversity, water quality, climate resilience, sustainable livelihoods, food systems, recreation, tourism, and community well-being. However, restoration projects are often technically and institutionally complex. Successful implementation may require cooperation among: Scientists and researchers Environmental authorities Local governments Conservation organizations Businesses and investors Marine and freshwater practitioners Community groups Citizen scientists Energy developers Landowners Fisheries and aquaculture stakeholders Civil society organizations Funding institutions Restoration professionals must understand ecological processes, but they may also need skills in stakeholder engagement, monitoring, project design, policy implementation, business planning, and funding. The Nature Restoration Academy has been structured around this practical reality. Its combination of scientific content, case studies, workshops, simulations, and financing discussions is intended to help participants understand how restoration projects move from ideas and policies to implementation. Structure of the Nature Restoration Academy The programme consists of three connected components. 1. Online Baseline Session Selected participants must first attend an online baseline session on October 6, 2026. The session will provide a common foundation before the in-person event. It will draw on relevant material from the Blue Bio Techpreneurs course, Integrated Ocean Planning: Marine Protected Areas, Multi-Use and Business Pathways . This common starting point should enable participants from different educational and professional backgrounds to take part more effectively in the advanced discussions and workshops held in Berlin. The application form specifically asks candidates to confirm whether they can attend the October 6 online session. Selected applicants are expected to participate in both the online and in-person components. 2. Two-Day Training Event in Berlin The main in-person programme will take place at the SUBMARINER Network’s Berlin office on October 29 and 30, 2026. The two-day event will combine: Lectures delivered by programme partners and invited experts Marine and freshwater restoration case studies Practical and interactive workshops Discussions on nature-based restoration approaches A multi-stakeholder negotiation simulation Digital monitoring and citizen-science content Sessions on project funding and business models A dedicated discussion on gender equality within the sector The limited cohort of 30 participants is likely to support active engagement, group work, peer learning, and direct interaction with trainers and other participants. 3. New Online Restoration Module Sessions delivered during the Berlin event will be recorded and used to develop a new online restoration module. The module will be added to the Blue Bio Techpreneurs course hosted on FutureLearn. This will allow the lessons, case studies, and expertise shared in Berlin to reach a much larger international audience after the in-person event. When announcing the Academy, SUBMARINER reported that the existing course had already reached 464 learners from more than 80 countries. The linked FutureLearn course provides theoretical foundations in marine protected areas, maritime spatial planning, ocean multi-use, conservation governance, business planning, and sustainable blue-economy development. The Nature Restoration Academy adds a more practical, in-person restoration component to this existing learning framework. Main Training Topics The programme will cover a broad selection of issues affecting the planning, implementation, monitoring, and financial sustainability of restoration projects. Nature-Based Solutions Participants will examine how nature-based solutions can be used to restore marine and freshwater ecosystems. Nature-based solutions generally work with natural ecological processes to address environmental and social challenges. Within aquatic restoration, these approaches may involve rebuilding ecosystem functions, improving habitat quality, strengthening biodiversity, or increasing resilience to environmental pressures. The Academy will connect these concepts with practical marine and freshwater restoration work. European Restoration Case Studies Real restoration case studies from Europe will be used to demonstrate how projects are designed and implemented in practice. Case-based learning can help participants understand: How restoration priorities are selected Which stakeholders need to be involved How ecological objectives are translated into activities What implementation challenges may arise How project results can be monitored Which lessons can be transferred to other locations These examples should allow participants to compare restoration strategies across different ecosystems and institutional settings. Citizen Science The programme will explore the role of citizen science in restoration. Citizen science can involve members of the public in observing environmental changes, collecting ecological data, reporting species, monitoring water conditions, or supporting long-term project evaluation. When properly designed, citizen-science programmes can expand monitoring capacity while improving public understanding and local ownership of restoration initiatives. Digital Monitoring Participants will also examine digital approaches to monitoring marine and freshwater restoration. Digital monitoring can help project teams collect, organize, analyse, and communicate environmental information more effectively. Depending on the project, this may include remote sensing, digital mapping, mobile data collection, automated sensors, databases, or online reporting systems. The Academy will consider how these tools can contribute to evidence-based restoration planning and evaluation. Restoration in Offshore Wind Parks One specialized topic will address restoration within offshore wind parks. The rapid development of offshore renewable energy creates both challenges and potential opportunities for marine ecosystems. Restoration and nature-inclusive planning must therefore consider the relationship between energy infrastructure, marine habitats, biodiversity, fishing activity, protected areas, and other uses of ocean space. This session should be particularly relevant to professionals interested in offshore renewable energy, marine spatial planning, environmental assessment, nature-inclusive design, and biodiversity protection. Business Models for Restoration The Academy will examine the business models that can support restoration activities over time. A restoration project may have a strong ecological justification but still struggle if it lacks a sustainable operational and financial structure. Participants will therefore consider how restoration initiatives can connect environmental objectives with viable delivery models. Relevant questions may include: Who finances the initial project? Who is responsible for long-term management? Which organizations benefit from restoration? Can ecosystem services be incorporated into the project model? How can public, private, philanthropic, and community resources be combined? How can restoration activities continue after short-term project funding ends? Funding Mechanisms Closely related to business-model development, the Academy will explore financing mechanisms for marine and freshwater restoration. This component is important because restoration projects may rely on multiple funding sources. These can include public programmes, environmental funds, foundations, private investment, corporate partnerships, research funding, community finance, or blended-finance arrangements. The training is expected to help participants understand that securing initial funding is only one part of project development. Long-term maintenance, monitoring, governance, and institutional ownership must also be considered. MPA Game: Multi-Stakeholder Negotiation Simulation The Berlin programme will include the MPA Game, an interactive simulation involving multi-stakeholder negotiation. MPA refers to a Marine Protected Area. Decisions concerning these areas may involve conservation authorities, local communities, researchers, fishing interests, tourism operators, energy developers, businesses, and other stakeholders. The simulation will allow participants to experience the challenges of balancing environmental protection with social and economic interests. It is designed to build skills in: Stakeholder analysis Negotiation Conflict management Collaborative decision-making Policy interpretation Communication Compromise and consensus-building Gender Equality in Marine and Freshwater Sectors The programme will include a dedicated gender-equality session delivered by WIN-BIG. This session will examine the importance of equal participation and opportunity within marine, freshwater, conservation, and blue-economy sectors. It will help participants consider how gender perspectives can be incorporated into environmental initiatives, professional development, decision-making, and sectoral leadership. Benefits of Participating Selected participants can expect several potential benefits from the programme: Free participation in a specialized restoration academy Practical training in marine and freshwater restoration Exposure to European restoration case studies Interaction with experts and practitioners Participation in workshops and negotiation simulations Knowledge of citizen-science and digital-monitoring approaches Better understanding of restoration business models Exposure to restoration funding mechanisms Learning related to offshore wind and nature-inclusive development A stronger understanding of stakeholder engagement Opportunities to connect with other early-career professionals, students, and practitioners Participation in discussions concerning gender equality in the sector A possible contribution toward travel expenses for participants travelling from outside Germany The programme announcement does not promise employment, a research grant, a stipend, or a fully funded trip. Its principal benefit is free access to the training programme and a possible contribution toward eligible travel costs. Participation Cost and Travel Support Participation in the Nature Restoration Academy is free of charge. Selected applicants will not be required to pay a programme registration or tuition fee. The organizers also state that a contribution toward travel costs is available for participants coming from outside Germany. Applicants should understand the wording carefully. A travel contribution is not necessarily the same as complete reimbursement. The announcement does not specify: The maximum travel contribution Whether all selected international participants will receive it Whether accommodation is covered Whether meals are covered Whether visa expenses are covered When travel funds will be paid Which transport methods are eligible Whether participants must pay first and claim reimbursement later The application form asks candidates to state: Where they will travel from The approximate distance to Berlin Their estimated travel cost Applicants who require financial assistance should provide an accurate and reasonable travel estimate. They should also request clarification from the organizers before making non-refundable travel arrangements. Who Should Consider Applying? The Academy is intended for people who are already engaged in, studying, or beginning a career connected to marine or freshwater restoration. Suitable backgrounds may include: Environmental science Marine biology Freshwater ecology Aquatic ecosystem management Conservation Biodiversity Marine protected areas Wetland restoration River or lake restoration Coastal management Environmental policy Marine spatial planning Citizen science Environmental monitoring Sustainable blue economy Offshore renewable energy Nature-based solutions Environmental project management Restoration finance Sustainability The organizers have not published a specific age limit, minimum degree requirement, mandatory number of years of experience, or required professional title. However, applicants should be able to demonstrate a credible connection to marine or freshwater restoration through their studies, work, research, projects, volunteering, or professional interests. Application Requirements Applicants must complete the official online form and provide the requested information. The form includes the following sections: Personal and Professional Information Applicants must provide: Full name Email address Organization or university Department or subject of study Professional sector Country of residence Nationality Gender Current role or professional profile The application form states that nationality and gender information will be used only for anonymized, aggregated reporting to EIT Water and will not be published with the applicant’s name. Motivation Statement Applicants must submit a short motivation statement. The online form provides a field with a 1,000-character limit. The statement should explain: Why the applicant wants to attend the Academy How their background relates to marine or freshwater restoration What they expect to learn How they will use the training What experience or perspective they can contribute Why they are a suitable candidate for one of the 30 places Because the available space is limited, applicants should avoid general statements and provide specific evidence of their interest or involvement. Short Curriculum Vitae Applicants must upload a short CV. The CV should prioritize information relevant to restoration, environmental science, conservation, policy, monitoring, sustainability, the blue economy, or related subjects. Relevant content may include: Education Current position or academic programme Environmental or restoration experience Research projects Relevant employment Internships Volunteer activities Publications Technical skills Community projects Professional memberships Training and certifications Attendance Confirmation Applicants must confirm whether they can attend the online baseline session on October 6, 2026. Selected participants are expected to attend both the online baseline session and the two-day event in Berlin. Candidates who cannot participate in both components may be less suitable for selection. Travel Information Applicants must identify: Their point of departure The approximate distance to Berlin The estimated cost of travelling to Berlin This information may help the organizers assess travel-support requirements for participants coming from outside Germany. Dietary and Accessibility Information The form allows applicants to disclose dietary requirements, including vegan, vegetarian, and gluten-free options. Applicants may also provide details of any accessibility requirements relevant to their participation. Data, Newsletter, and Media Information The application includes fields concerning: SUBMARINER Network newsletter updates Processing of personal data for event administration and anonymized reporting Photography and filming during the event The event will be photographed and filmed for promotional and educational purposes by EIT Water, the Poul Due Jensen Foundation, and the SUBMARINER Network. Recorded sessions will also contribute to the future online restoration module. Applicants should read the consent language and the SUBMARINER Network privacy policy carefully before submitting the form. How to Apply Applicants should complete the following steps: Review the official programme announcement. Confirm availability for the online session on October 6, 2026. Confirm availability to travel to Berlin for October 29–30, 2026. Prepare a concise motivation statement within the application field’s 1,000-character limit. Prepare a short, relevant CV. Estimate the travel distance and cost to Berlin. Complete all personal, academic, professional, dietary, accessibility, and consent sections. Review the information carefully. Submit the form before September 15, 2026. Applications must be submitted through the official Nature Restoration Academy application form . Important Dates Stage Date Application deadline September 15, 2026 Selection notification By October 1, 2026 Online baseline session October 6, 2026 In-person Berlin training October 29–30, 2026 The official announcement does not specify a deadline time or time zone. Applicants should therefore submit before the final date rather than waiting until the last few hours. Separate Opportunity for Lecturers and Workshop Leaders In addition to participant applications, the SUBMARINER Network is inviting restoration experts to contribute a lecture or case study to the Berlin programme. Potential contributors should: Have expertise in marine or freshwater restoration Be able to participate in person in Berlin Be prepared to deliver a session of approximately one hour Consider combining a short lecture with an interactive workshop Be willing for the session to be recorded and incorporated into the new FutureLearn restoration module Experts interested in contributing should contact the organizers at info@submariner-network.eu . This contributor invitation is separate from the standard application process for the 30 participant places. Tips for a Strong Application Because only 30 participants will be selected, applicants should make their relevance clear. A strong application should: Establish a direct connection with marine or freshwater restoration. Mention a specific academic, professional, research, or community project. Explain which Academy topics are most relevant to the applicant. Describe how the knowledge will be applied after the programme. Show an interest in practical implementation, not only theory. Demonstrate willingness to participate actively in workshops and simulations. Confirm availability for both programme components. Provide a concise and relevant CV. Give an accurate estimate of travel costs. Submit before the deadline. Applicants should not describe the programme as fully funded. Participation is free, and a travel contribution may be available for people travelling from outside Germany, but complete coverage of travel, accommodation, meals, visas, or other costs has not been announced. Conclusion The Nature Restoration Academy 2026 provides a valuable opportunity to develop practical skills in marine and freshwater ecosystem restoration through a combination of online learning, expert instruction, applied case studies, interactive workshops, and stakeholder simulation. The programme’s focus on nature-based solutions, citizen science, digital monitoring, offshore wind parks, restoration finance, business models, negotiation, and gender equality reflects the wide range of capabilities required to deliver successful environmental restoration projects. Participation is free, and a contribution toward travel expenses may be available for selected participants travelling from outside Germany. However, places are highly limited, with only 30 participants expected to join the programme. Eligible candidates should prepare a focused motivation statement and short CV, confirm that they can attend the October 6 online session and the October 29–30 Berlin event, and submit the official application by September 15, 2026. title: South African Master in Ocean Sciences (AOS-SAMOS) 2027: Fully Interdisciplinary Master’s Programme for Aspiring Ocean Professionals
summary: The South African Master in Ocean Sciences (AOS-SAMOS) is an innovative postgraduate programme designed to strengthen Ocean Sciences education, research capacity and professional opportunities in South Africa while supporting the sustainable development of the country’s growing Blue Economy. The programme brings together nine South African universities, national research institutions and European academic partners to create an internationally recognised, interdisciplinary Master’s degree that combines ocean science, marine biology, oceanography, quantitative analysis, digital technologies, social sciences, law, humanities and sustainability. Applications for the 2027 AOS-SAMOS cohort are currently open , with a maximum intake of 30 students . The application deadline is Sunday, 31 August 2026 . What Is the South African Master in Ocean Sciences? The South African Master in Ocean Sciences is a collaborative postgraduate initiative developed in response to the increasing importance of oceans and coastal environments to South Africa’s economy, environment and society. South Africa faces a range of interconnected challenges affecting its marine and coastal systems, including: Climate change and global warming Biodiversity loss Overfishing and over-exploitation of marine resources Coastal development and urbanisation Environmental degradation Water-quality challenges Sustainable fisheries and food security Marine conservation Environmental governance The need for better scientific data and forecasting The sustainable development of the Blue Economy These challenges require professionals who can understand the ocean from multiple perspectives rather than from a single academic discipline. AOS-SAMOS therefore provides an interdisciplinary training environment in which students can develop the scientific, analytical, research, digital and professional skills needed to contribute to modern Ocean Sciences and sustainable development. The programme is also designed to strengthen collaboration between South African universities and European partners while improving postgraduate teaching and research capacity, particularly at Historically Disadvantaged Universities (HDUs). Why Was the SAMOS Programme Created? South Africa has significant marine and coastal resources, but there has historically been limited access to comprehensive, interdisciplinary postgraduate education in Ocean Sciences. The SAMOS project was created to address this gap by bringing together the expertise and infrastructure of universities and research institutions across South Africa. The programme seeks to: Modernise postgraduate Ocean Sciences education in South Africa. Improve the quality and relevance of higher education in Ocean Sciences. Increase graduate employability. Prepare professionals capable of addressing major environmental and socioeconomic challenges. Strengthen teaching and research capacities at Historically Disadvantaged Universities. Build stronger networks between South African and European universities. Establish a major centre of Ocean Sciences expertise in the Eastern Cape. Support research and innovation relevant to the sustainable Blue Economy. Promote inclusive and interdisciplinary education. Contribute to Sustainable Development Goals relating to education, gender equality, climate action, life below water, equality and global partnerships. The programme is supported through the Erasmus+ Capacity Building in Higher Education framework and is co-funded by the European Union under Grant Agreement No. 101179091. A Truly Interdisciplinary Ocean Sciences Programme One of the major strengths of AOS-SAMOS is its interdisciplinary approach. Rather than limiting students to one narrow area of marine science, the programme integrates different fields that are increasingly important for understanding and managing marine and coastal systems. The curriculum brings together areas including: Physical oceanography Chemical oceanography Marine biology Applied marine biology Operational oceanography Marine social sciences Environmental sustainability Law and humanities Earth observation Satellite oceanography Quantitative analysis Scientific programming Bioinformatics Geographical Information Systems Data visualisation Marine conservation Environmental monitoring Research methodology Professional and collaborative skills The programme is intentionally interdisciplinary and Afro-centric, with an emphasis on applying Ocean Sciences to challenges relevant to South Africa and the wider African region. Programme Structure The AOS-SAMOS degree is a full-time taught Master’s programme worth 180 credits . It consists of: 90 credits of coursework 90 credits for a minor dissertation The programme is scheduled to commence in February 2027 for the 2027 cohort. The coursework component is expected to run over approximately 24 weeks between February and August 2027 at the Nelson Mandela University Ocean Sciences Campus in Gqeberha. Students are required to attend the coursework in person. Depending on the funding and study pathway, the degree can be completed over one or two years. Students receiving SAMOS-NRF funding follow a two-year curriculum, allowing the dissertation component to be completed during the second year. Self-funded students may have the option of following a 13-month pathway with the minor dissertation at the University of Cape Town. Where Will Students Study? Applications for the 2027 programme are managed through a single-entry point at the University of Cape Town (UCT) . The coursework is delivered at the Nelson Mandela University Ocean Sciences Campus in Gqeberha, Eastern Cape . Students subsequently undertake their minor dissertation through one of the participating South African partner universities, depending on their research area and supervisory arrangements. The Ocean Sciences Campus provides access to specialised facilities, research infrastructure and a network of researchers working across marine and environmental disciplines. Facilities and research entities associated with the campus include areas such as: Marine and coastal research Marine robotics Environmental observation Coastal palaeosciences Marine and fisheries research Maritime education and research Environmental monitoring Hyperbaric research infrastructure This gives students the opportunity to combine classroom-based postgraduate education with practical research and exposure to real-world marine science. What Will Students Learn? The curriculum is designed to prepare graduates for professional and research careers across the Ocean Sciences sector. Students are expected to develop the ability to: Apply a whole-systems approach to sustainability in an ocean sciences context. Understand regional marine ecosystems and their dynamics. Collect and analyse Ocean Sciences data using quantitative techniques. Develop and conduct research projects addressing theoretical or practical problems. Apply advanced analytical and computational tools. Work with models and data relevant to Ocean Sciences. Use emerging technologies and tools in marine research. Monitor environmental change and assess the impacts of human activities. Examine sustainable development across different economic sectors. Analyse emerging threats and opportunities affecting ocean sustainability. Work effectively in multidisciplinary teams. These skills are intended to prepare graduates for both research-oriented and professional careers in the Blue Economy. Key Areas of the Curriculum 1. Applied Ocean Sciences The programme provides students with a broad foundation in applied Ocean Sciences, enabling them to understand how marine systems operate and how scientific knowledge can be applied to real-world environmental and socioeconomic challenges. 2. Marine Biology Students can develop knowledge relevant to marine organisms, ecosystems, biodiversity and the management and conservation of marine resources. 3. Operational Oceanography Operational Oceanography focuses on observing, understanding and predicting marine conditions. Students are introduced to the use of satellite observations, in-situ measurements and numerical models to generate information that can support decision-making in science, government and industry. 4. Earth Observation and Satellite Oceanography Earth Observation provides tools for monitoring marine environments on large spatial scales. Students explore concepts including satellite sensing, electromagnetic radiation, ocean-light interactions and the use of remote sensing technologies for understanding marine environments. 5. Advanced Data Analysis The programme also provides training in advanced analytical and computational techniques. Depending on the area selected, students may work with: Bioinformatics Geographical Information Systems Multivariate analysis Scientific programming Satellite oceanography High-performance computing Advanced data visualisation Students gain practical experience applying these tools to real datasets. 6. Minor Dissertation The 90-credit minor dissertation allows students to undertake substantial research in a selected area of Ocean Sciences. Students may conduct their research across different disciplines offered by the SAMOS partner universities and are generally based at the university of their principal supervisor. Applicants seeking NRF funding are required to identify a potential supervisor and research project before submitting their funding application. Who Can Apply? AOS-SAMOS is designed for qualified postgraduate applicants who have an academic background relevant to the programme. The programme welcomes applicants from both natural sciences and social sciences/humanities , although preference is given to applicants with a strong science background and demonstrated numerical skills. Previous specialised knowledge of oceanography or marine biology is not essential . Applicants should generally have: A four-year Bachelor’s degree that includes a research project; or An Honours degree; or Another equivalent NQF Level 8 qualification; The qualification must include a 30-credit research component and demonstrate disciplinary alignment with the AOS-SAMOS curriculum; An average of at least 65% in science subjects, or above 70% in other pertinent subjects; A strong academic record; A demonstrated interest in marine science; Good numeracy skills are strongly recommended. Applicants without a natural sciences background must explain in their motivation letter how they intend to address gaps in natural science and numerical knowledge. Can Applicants Without a Science Degree Apply? Yes. This is one of the distinctive features of AOS-SAMOS. The programme does not restrict eligibility exclusively to traditional marine science, oceanography or biology graduates. Applicants from social sciences and humanities backgrounds can be considered, provided they meet the relevant academic requirements. However, applicants without a natural sciences background are expected to demonstrate how they will compensate for gaps in science and quantitative knowledge. This makes the programme potentially relevant to graduates whose previous studies include areas such as environmental policy, economics, development studies, law, governance, geography, social sciences and related disciplines, subject to the programme s academic requirements and disciplinary alignment. English Language Requirements English is the language of instruction and examination. Applicants must provide evidence of English-language proficiency. For South African applicants, acceptable evidence includes the relevant English qualification through the National Senior Certificate or Senior Certificate. International applicants can demonstrate English proficiency through recognised tests such as: TOEFL IELTS National Benchmark Test Academic Literacy The published requirements include a minimum IELTS overall band score of 7.0 , with no individual component below 6.0 . For TOEFL, the stated minimums include: 570 for the paper-based test 230 for the computer-based test 88 for the internet-based test Applicants should check the official requirements before applying because documentation and testing requirements can vary depending on individual circumstances. International Applicants The programme is not restricted exclusively to South African citizens. The official requirements page provides a pathway for international applicants, including applicants from outside South Africa. International applicants must satisfy the academic and English-language requirements and must also contact the University of Cape Town s International Academic Programmes Office for guidance on the documentation required to study in South Africa. The programme therefore has potential relevance to applicants from across Africa and beyond, although admission is competitive and subject to the stated academic requirements and available places. How Competitive Is the Programme? AOS-SAMOS has a maximum intake of 30 students for the 2027 cohort. This means applicants should not treat meeting the minimum academic requirements as an automatic guarantee of admission. Applicants should prepare a strong application that clearly demonstrates: Academic achievement Interest in Ocean Sciences Relevant experience Research interests Career objectives Understanding of the programme Quantitative and analytical ability Potential research direction Ability to work collaboratively The motivation letter is particularly important because it gives applicants an opportunity to explain their academic background, experience, reasons for applying and research interests. Application Documents Applicants should prepare the required supporting documentation carefully. The official application guidance lists: Curriculum Vitae, limited to two pages Proof of highest qualification Academic transcripts Motivation letter Relevant information concerning academic background and experience Research interests Identified supervisor and research project where applicable Applicants applying for the SAMOS-NRF bursary must identify a potential supervisor and research project before applying for the funding. They may also need to provide a reference letter from a current supervisor, course convenor or Head of Department addressing academic performance, research ability, reliability, professionalism, disciplinary history, readiness for Master s-level study and ability to work in a collaborative environment. Incomplete applications will not be considered. Application Deadline For the 2027 AOS-SAMOS Master’s programme , applications are currently open and will close on: Sunday, 31 August 2026 There are only 30 available places , making it important for prospective applicants to submit complete applications before the closing date. Important Funding Deadline The programme application and funding application are separate processes. For the 2027 academic year, applicants seeking the DSTI-NRF Master s Student Funding were invited to apply through NRF Connect by the UCT internal closing date of 26 June 2026 . The SAMOS programme website states that 10 bursaries are available through this call, subject to NRF eligibility requirements and funding decisions. Acceptance into SAMOS does not automatically guarantee funding. Therefore, applicants should distinguish between: The AOS-SAMOS programme application deadline: 31 August 2026 The 2027 DSTI-NRF funding deadline: 26 June 2026 Applicants who are specifically interested in funding should check the latest official funding information rather than assuming that admission automatically includes a scholarship. Funding and Financial Support AOS-SAMOS is not automatically a fully funded Master s programme for every admitted student. The programme provides information about several potential funding sources, including the DSTI-NRF Master s Student Funding scheme and other postgraduate funding opportunities. South African students and permanent residents may be considered for Full Cost of Study or Partial Cost of Study funding, subject to the relevant eligibility criteria and availability of funding. International students may qualify for Partial Cost of Study funding, although the number of international scholarships is limited. The programme therefore encourages applicants to investigate multiple funding sources and to consider self-funding where necessary. Programme Fees The published 2026 fee structure provides an indication of the programme s costs. For South African students, the stated total is approximately R78,300 , consisting of coursework and dissertation fees. For SADC students, the published total is approximately R83,900 , including the applicable administrative fee. For non-SADC African students, the published total is approximately R132,100 . For international students from outside Africa, the published total is approximately R148,400 . These figures are based on the published fee information and should not be assumed to be the final 2027 fees. The programme advises applicants to check the updated fee information for the relevant academic year. Accommodation Students are expected to attend the coursework component physically at Nelson Mandela University s Ocean Sciences Campus in Gqeberha. Accommodation is the responsibility of successful students. Nelson Mandela University provides assistance to students looking for suitable off-campus accommodation, but applicants should plan their accommodation and living expenses separately from tuition and other academic costs. Career Opportunities After the Programme The AOS-SAMOS programme is designed to improve graduate employability and prepare students for careers connected to the sustainable Blue Economy. Potential areas of employment and professional development include: Oceanography Marine biology Marine conservation Environmental consulting Coastal management Fisheries and marine-resource management Environmental monitoring Ocean observation Satellite and Earth Observation Marine data analysis Scientific programming Marine policy Environmental governance Research institutions Government agencies Non-governmental organisations Maritime and ocean-related industries Sustainability and environmental consulting Academic and research careers The programme s emphasis on interdisciplinary knowledge, quantitative skills, digital tools, research and professional collaboration is intended to help graduates respond to both scientific and socioeconomic challenges within the Blue Economy. Why the Programme Matters for Africa Africa s oceans represent an enormous source of economic, environmental and social potential. Marine ecosystems support fisheries, tourism, transport, coastal communities, food systems and other economic activities. At the same time, these systems are increasingly threatened by climate change, biodiversity loss, pollution, unsustainable exploitation and poorly managed development. Building a highly skilled generation of African ocean professionals is therefore essential. AOS-SAMOS contributes to this objective by creating a postgraduate training environment that connects scientific knowledge with policy, technology, conservation, business and sustainable development. The programme s focus on collaboration between South African institutions and European partners also provides an opportunity to strengthen international academic networks and research cooperation. A Strong Opportunity for Interdisciplinary Graduates A particularly important aspect of AOS-SAMOS is that applicants do not necessarily need to come from a conventional marine science background. The programme recognises that solving complex ocean problems requires people with different perspectives. A graduate with a strong background in science may contribute advanced technical knowledge, while someone from the social sciences, humanities, law, policy or another related field may contribute expertise in governance, human behaviour, economics, policy or societal impacts. This multidisciplinary approach reflects the reality that ocean challenges cannot be solved through science alone. How to Apply Prospective applicants should begin by reviewing the official AOS-SAMOS admission requirements and preparing their supporting documents. The application process involves: Reviewing the eligibility requirements. Preparing a suitable CV of no more than two pages. Obtaining proof of the highest qualification. Preparing complete academic transcripts. Writing a strong motivation letter. Clearly explaining academic and professional experience. Describing research interests. Selecting preferred study streams. Identifying a prospective supervisor and research project if applying for SAMOS-NRF funding. Submitting the application through the University of Cape Town s application system. Ensuring all supporting documents are submitted. Completing the application before the 31 August 2026 deadline . Applicants should carefully verify all requirements before submission because incomplete applications will not be considered. Study Streams Applicants applying through UCT are instructed to select the relevant Master s qualification and choose their preferred stream. The two listed options are: Applied Ocean Sciences (Applied Marine Biology) Applied Ocean Sciences (Operational Oceanography) Applicants are required to indicate their first and second choices during the application process. title: The National Lottery Community Fund Grants 2026: UK Community Funding Opportunities for Stronger, Fairer Communities
summary: The National Lottery Community Fund is a major source of community funding in the United Kingdom, supporting projects designed to help people connect, develop, overcome disadvantage and create stronger communities. Through funding generated by the National Lottery, the organisation supports community-led initiatives that seek to make a meaningful and lasting difference to people s lives. Its overall focus is on building stronger, fairer and more inclusive communities , with particular attention given to people experiencing poverty, disadvantage or discrimination. The National Lottery Community Fund has set an ambitious long-term goal: by 2030, it plans to distribute more than £4 billion to help create stronger and fairer communities across the UK. This makes the fund an important potential source of support for organisations, community groups and initiatives working to address social, economic, environmental and wellbeing challenges. Rather than focusing on only one type of project, the organisation supports a broad range of community-led activities. These can include initiatives that bring people together, improve outcomes for children and young people, strengthen physical and emotional wellbeing, protect the environment and help communities respond to climate change. What Is The National Lottery Community Fund? The National Lottery Community Fund is the UK s largest community funder, distributing money raised through National Lottery funding to support projects that benefit communities. Its approach is strongly centred on community-led change . This means that the organisation backs projects developed around the needs, priorities and aspirations of local communities. The fund s work is based on the understanding that communities can create better outcomes when people have opportunities to: Build meaningful connections with one another. Reduce isolation and loneliness. Create welcoming and inclusive community spaces. Support children and young people to thrive. Improve physical, mental and emotional wellbeing. Protect nature and the environment. Respond to environmental challenges and climate change. Address poverty, disadvantage and discrimination. Develop stronger and more resilient communities. For organisations seeking community funding in the UK, understanding these priorities is important because successful projects are expected to demonstrate how their work can contribute to positive outcomes for people and communities. National Lottery Community Fund s Long-Term Vision The organisation s overarching vision is built around the belief that stronger communities create brighter futures . Its funding strategy therefore places community-led initiatives at the centre of its work. Rather than simply providing financial support, the fund aims to contribute to broader social change by investing in projects that can improve people s experiences and strengthen communities. By 2030, the National Lottery Community Fund intends to share over £4 billion to help build stronger and fairer communities throughout the United Kingdom. This long-term commitment creates significant opportunities for community organisations and groups whose projects align with the fund s priorities. The Four Community-Led Missions The National Lottery Community Fund has identified four major community-led missions that guide the outcomes it wants to see from the projects it supports. These missions provide an important framework for understanding the types of projects that may be relevant to its funding programmes. 1. Communities Come Together The first mission focuses on helping communities become more connected, welcoming and inclusive. Social connection is an important part of building healthy communities. Projects under this broad area can help people develop relationships, participate in community activities and feel that they belong. The fund highlights outcomes such as: Building stronger connections between people. Reducing loneliness and social isolation. Creating spaces where people feel welcome. Encouraging participation in community activities. Helping people develop stronger relationships within their communities. Creating opportunities for people from different backgrounds to interact and work together. Community organisations working to tackle loneliness, isolation or social exclusion may therefore find this mission particularly relevant. The emphasis is not simply on bringing people together for individual events. The broader objective is to create stronger and more connected communities where people feel included and able to participate. 2. Communities Help Children and Young People Thrive The second mission focuses on babies, children and young people . The National Lottery Community Fund recognises that communities can play an important role in helping younger people grow, connect and build positive futures. Projects in this area may seek to improve opportunities and outcomes for children and young people by helping them: Develop relationships and social connections. Participate in positive community activities. Access supportive environments. Build confidence and skills. Feel connected to their communities. Develop healthier and brighter futures. Organisations working with children, young people and families should therefore consider how their proposed project could demonstrate meaningful and measurable benefits for its participants. 3. Communities Are Healthier The third mission focuses on community health and wellbeing. Health is considered broadly within this mission, including physical, mental and emotional wellbeing . Projects can contribute to healthier communities by creating opportunities for people to become more active, improve their wellbeing, access supportive environments and develop healthier lifestyles. Potential areas of relevance include: Physical wellbeing. Mental wellbeing. Emotional wellbeing. Community-based health initiatives. Activities that encourage healthier lifestyles. Programmes that help people participate in supportive social environments. Initiatives designed to improve overall community wellbeing. Projects addressing health and wellbeing challenges should clearly explain the problem they are responding to and demonstrate how their activities could result in positive outcomes for the people involved. 4. Communities Are Environmentally Sustainable The fourth mission focuses on environmental sustainability and the ability of communities to respond to environmental challenges. The National Lottery Community Fund is interested in projects that can help communities protect nature, reduce environmental harm and respond to climate change. Relevant initiatives may include projects focused on: Protecting nature. Improving local environments. Reducing environmental harm. Community sustainability. Responding to climate change. Encouraging environmentally responsible behaviour. Helping communities become more resilient to environmental challenges. This means environmental and climate-focused community projects may be able to align with the fund s sustainability priorities where they demonstrate clear community benefits. Who Can Benefit From The Funding? The National Lottery Community Fund is focused on community projects rather than personal financial support for individuals . Its funding is intended to support initiatives that create positive outcomes for people and communities across the UK. The organisation places particular emphasis on supporting people experiencing: Poverty. Disadvantage. Discrimination. Social isolation. Other barriers that can prevent people from participating fully in community life. A strong project proposal should therefore demonstrate a clear community need and explain how the proposed activities will address that need. Applicants should also show that their project is genuinely connected to the community it intends to serve. Where Is The Funding Available? The National Lottery Community Fund operates across the United Kingdom. Its website identifies four geographical funding areas: England Northern Ireland Scotland Wales However, applicants should not assume that every funding programme has identical geographical eligibility requirements. Different programmes can have different rules concerning location, applicant type, project size, eligible activities and funding amounts. Applicants should therefore check the specific requirements of the programme they intend to apply for before preparing a full application. What Types of Projects Could Be Relevant? Because the National Lottery Community Fund operates multiple funding programmes, the precise activities supported can vary. Nevertheless, the organisation s four missions provide a useful indication of the broad areas in which community projects may have potential relevance. Examples of potentially relevant project themes include: Community connection projects These may include initiatives designed to: Reduce loneliness. Bring residents together. Build community relationships. Create inclusive spaces. Encourage participation. Support people who are socially isolated. Children and youth projects These may include initiatives that: Support young people. Improve community participation. Provide positive activities. Build confidence and connections. Help children and young people develop. Strengthen support networks for younger people. Health and wellbeing projects These may include programmes focused on: Physical activity. Mental wellbeing. Emotional wellbeing. Healthy lifestyles. Community-based wellbeing. Social activities that contribute to healthier communities. Environmental projects These may include initiatives focused on: Nature conservation. Community environmental action. Climate change. Sustainability. Reducing environmental damage. Improving local natural spaces. These examples should be treated as broad areas of alignment rather than a guarantee that a particular activity will qualify for funding. Applicants should always check the eligibility criteria for the specific funding programme. Why Community Organisations Should Consider This Funding The scale and breadth of the National Lottery Community Fund make it a potentially important funding source for eligible community initiatives across the UK. One of the major advantages is that the organisation does not focus on a single social issue. Instead, its four missions cover several areas that are central to community development: Social connection. Children and young people. Health and wellbeing. Environmental sustainability. The fund also has a strong focus on communities experiencing poverty, disadvantage and discrimination. This makes it particularly relevant to organisations that are developing projects to address real community needs rather than simply seeking funding for general organisational expenses. How To Find The Right National Lottery Community Fund Programme The National Lottery Community Fund provides a dedicated section where applicants can browse its funding programmes. This is an important stage of the application process because there is not necessarily one universal grant application that applies to every organisation or project. Applicants should review the available programmes and filter them according to relevant criteria. When looking for a suitable programme, consider: Your project s location Confirm that your project operates in an eligible part of the UK. The type of organisation applying Check whether the programme accepts your particular organisation or community group structure. The people your project supports Clearly identify who benefits from your work. The community problem you are addressing Explain why the project is needed and what challenge it seeks to solve. Your project s objectives Establish what you want to achieve through the funding. The relevant community mission Consider whether your project contributes to stronger connections, better outcomes for children and young people, healthier communities or environmental sustainability. The programme s individual requirements Read the full eligibility rules, application guidance and funding conditions before applying. Preparing A Strong Application Getting ready before beginning an application can significantly improve the quality of a funding proposal. The National Lottery Community Fund provides guidance designed to help applicants understand the funding process and complete applications with greater confidence. Before applying, organisations should consider preparing the following information. A clear description of the project Explain what the project is, what activities will take place and how the project will operate. Avoid describing the idea only in general terms. Give the funder a practical understanding of what will happen if funding is awarded. Evidence of community need Explain the problem that the project is designed to address. A strong proposal should answer questions such as: What problem exists? Who is affected? Why is the issue important? What evidence demonstrates the need? Why is the proposed project an appropriate response? Clearly identified beneficiaries Explain who will benefit from the project. This may involve identifying a particular community, age group or population experiencing disadvantage, isolation, poverty or another challenge. Expected outcomes Explain what will change as a result of the project. For example, a project may aim to increase community participation, reduce loneliness, improve wellbeing, help young people develop stronger connections or increase community involvement in environmental sustainability. A realistic implementation plan Show how the project will be delivered. This can include: Key activities. Project stages. Staffing or volunteers. Community partners. Resources required. Monitoring and evaluation. Expected timescales. A realistic budget Applicants should carefully consider how much funding is needed and how the money will be used. A clear budget helps demonstrate that the proposed project has been thoughtfully planned. The Funding Journey The National Lottery Community Fund describes the funding process as a journey that moves from an initial idea through application and, if successful, into delivery of the funded project. The organisation provides guidance across several stages. Stage 1: Develop your idea Start by identifying a genuine community need and developing a project that responds to it. Stage 2: Get ready to apply Review the available guidance and determine which funding programme best fits the project. Stage 3: Submit an application Complete the relevant application process and provide the requested information. Stage 4: Wait for the funding decision The application will be considered according to the relevant programme s requirements and assessment process. Stage 5: Start the funded project If funding is awarded, the organisation can begin delivering the approved activities in accordance with the grant conditions. Stage 6: Manage and report on the funding Successful applicants may need to report on progress, demonstrate how funding has been used and communicate the impact of their work. This means receiving a grant is not the end of the process. Funded organisations have responsibilities for managing the funding and demonstrating progress. Successful organisations should therefore ensure that they understand their responsibilities after receiving funding. Keeping accurate records, monitoring activities and documenting outcomes can help organisations demonstrate the impact of their project. Important Funding Priorities Applicants should pay particular attention to the organisation s emphasis on poverty, disadvantage and discrimination . These issues form an important part of the fund s wider purpose. A project is likely to be stronger when it can clearly demonstrate: The community challenge it is addressing. The people affected by that challenge. Why those people need support. How the project will respond. What positive outcomes are expected. How the community will be involved. How the results will be measured. Community-led approaches are particularly important because the fund s strategy places local people and communities at the centre of its work. The government is seeking public views on how this funding should be distributed. The National Lottery Community Fund encourages people interested in community funding to learn more about the consultation and have their say. This is separate from applying for a grant, but it provides an opportunity for people and organisations interested in community development to contribute to discussions about the future direction of National Lottery funding. These updates demonstrate the range of community issues being addressed through National Lottery Community Fund-supported initiatives. Is There A Deadline To Apply? No single deadline is stated on the information provided. This is important because the page presented is the main National Lottery Community Fund website rather than a single grant programme with one application closing date. The organisation has multiple funding programmes, and individual programmes may have different: Opening dates. Closing dates. Application windows. Eligibility criteria. Funding amounts. Assessment procedures. Applicants should therefore identify the specific programme that fits their project and check its individual deadline before submitting an application. Do not assume that a deadline associated with one National Lottery Community Fund programme applies to all funding opportunities. How To Improve Your Chances Of Submitting A Strong Proposal Although eligibility and assessment criteria depend on the individual funding programme, applicants can take several practical steps when preparing a community funding proposal. 1. Start with the community need Do not begin with the amount of money you want. Begin by explaining the problem affecting the community and why action is needed. 2. Be specific about outcomes Instead of simply saying that a project will help the community , explain exactly what positive changes you expect to achieve. 4. Connect the project to the relevant mission Clearly demonstrate how your project contributes to one or more of the National Lottery Community Fund s four missions. 5. Demonstrate inclusion If your project supports people experiencing disadvantage, poverty, discrimination or isolation, explain this clearly and show how the project will remove barriers to participation. 6. Create a realistic budget Request an amount that is appropriate for the project s activities and clearly explain how the funding will be used. 7. Read the programme-specific guidance This is one of the most important steps. The overall National Lottery Community Fund strategy provides broad direction, but the exact requirements for an application depend on the particular funding programme. How To Access National Lottery Community Fund Opportunities Applicants interested in community funding should explore the organisation s funding programmes and identify the opportunity that best matches their project. Conclusion The National Lottery Community Fund offers an important funding route for community-led projects across the UK. With a long-term commitment to distributing more than £4 billion by 2030, the fund has positioned community development, inclusion and social impact at the heart of its strategy. Its four community-led missions provide a clear indication of the types of positive change it wants to support: bringing communities together, helping children and young people thrive, creating healthier communities and promoting environmental sustainability.
