title: Gilder Lehrman Scholarly Fellowships 2026: $3,000 for American History Research in New York City
summary: Applications are now open for the Gilder Lehrman Institute Scholarly Fellowships 2026 , offering short-term research funding to doctoral candidates, university and college faculty members, and independent scholars conducting research in the field of American history. The Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History awards annual short-term research fellowships valued at $3,000 each to support scholars who need to conduct research using historical collections and resources in New York City. For the 2026 competition, the Institute expects to award ten Gilder Lehrman Scholarly Fellowships . While research projects covering all aspects of American history are eligible, the Institute has identified three areas that will receive particular attention during the current application cycle: Colonial American history Slavery and abolition studies Cold War studies Three of the ten fellowships are specifically connected to these priority fields: John Winthrop Fellowship with a Focus on Colonial History Scholarly Fellowship in Slavery and Abolition Studies Scholarly Fellowship in Cold War Studies Preference will be given to strong applications in these fields, but researchers working on other periods and subjects in American history are still encouraged to apply. The fellowship is open internationally. Eligible applicants include doctoral candidates, academic faculty members at every rank, and independent scholars. Successful applicants must complete their funded research in New York City within one year of notification of the award . Applications must be submitted online by 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on Monday, October 26, 2026 . About the Gilder Lehrman Institute Scholarly Fellowships The Gilder Lehrman Institute provides its Scholarly Fellowships to support researchers undertaking original work in American history. The programme has a long record of supporting historians and other scholars at different stages of their academic careers. Since the fellowship programme began in 1994, the Institute has awarded 723 fellowships . Rather than limiting support exclusively to established professors, the programme deliberately includes several categories of researchers: Doctoral candidates College faculty University faculty Independent scholars International scholars This makes the fellowship particularly valuable for researchers who need relatively short-term financial assistance to complete archival research connected with a dissertation, book project, article, or other substantial scholarly work. Fellowship Value Each Gilder Lehrman Scholarly Fellowship provides: $3,000 The fellowship is designed as short-term research support. The Institute does not describe the award as a full scholarship covering every cost associated with travel, accommodation, and living expenses. Applicants are therefore required to include an anticipated budget within their project proposal explaining how they expect to use the fellowship funds. Researchers should plan carefully for costs associated with conducting research in New York City. Number of Fellowships Available For the 2026 competition, the Gilder Lehrman Institute plans to award: Ten Scholarly Fellowships Among these ten awards, three are linked to specific thematic research priorities. The remaining fellowships remain open to high-quality research covering the broader field of American history. Research Field: American History The programme is specifically intended for scholars working in: American history The Institute welcomes applications examining a wide variety of themes, periods, populations, institutions, movements, events, and historical processes. Although the 2026 call gives preference to three particular fields, applicants should not assume that projects outside those areas are ineligible. The official call explicitly states that: Projects on all aspects of American history are welcome. This creates opportunities for researchers working across a broad range of subjects. Potential fields may include political, social, cultural, economic, diplomatic, military, intellectual, legal, gender, labor, racial, transnational, or environmental history, provided the project makes a meaningful contribution to the study of American history. Special Priority Area 1: Colonial American History One of the special awards available in 2026 is the: John Winthrop Fellowship with a Focus on Colonial History The fellowship specifically supports research concerning the colonial era. The award is funded by John Winthrop, a descendant of John Winthrop, the first governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony . The Gilder Lehrman Collection includes an important 1634 letter written by Winthrop describing life in Boston, helping connect the fellowship with the Institute s historical holdings. Researchers whose work focuses on colonial America may therefore have a particularly strong opportunity during the 2026 competition. Relevant research could potentially engage with topics such as: Colonial government Indigenous-colonial relations Religion Migration Atlantic history Settlement Law Gender Labor Trade Race Political culture Everyday life Applicants should still formulate an original research project rather than relying only on the broad priority area. Special Priority Area 2: Slavery and Abolition Studies The Institute is also offering a: Scholarly Fellowship in Slavery and Abolition Studies Projects examining the histories of slavery, emancipation, resistance, abolition, race, African American communities, and related themes may receive particular consideration. This priority reflects the importance of slavery and abolition to understanding American political, social, economic, and cultural development. Researchers could potentially work with archival material concerning: Enslaved people Abolitionist organizations Resistance Slaveholding societies Emancipation Reconstruction African American communities Political debates Legal structures Memory of slavery The exact research question remains up to the applicant. Special Priority Area 3: Cold War Studies The third designated fellowship is the: Scholarly Fellowship in Cold War Studies Researchers studying the Cold War and its political, military, social, diplomatic, technological, cultural, or ideological dimensions are encouraged to apply. Potential topics could include: U.S. foreign policy Nuclear politics Civil defense International relations Anti-communism Propaganda Intelligence Domestic politics Civil rights Cultural diplomacy Scientific competition Projects do not necessarily need to follow traditional diplomatic-history approaches if they contribute meaningfully to understanding the American experience of the Cold War. Other American History Topics Remain Eligible Applicants should not interpret the three special fellowships as meaning that only colonial history, slavery and abolition, or Cold War research will be funded. The Institute explicitly states that: All areas of American history remain eligible. The thematic priorities simply mean that applications in those three fields may receive particular attention. A strong project outside the priority areas can still compete for one of the general Gilder Lehrman Scholarly Fellowships. Who Can Apply? The Gilder Lehrman Scholarly Fellowships are open to three principal groups. 1. Doctoral Candidates Current PhD candidates working on American history can apply. This may be especially useful for doctoral researchers who: Need additional archival material Are completing dissertation chapters Need to verify primary sources Are developing a substantial dissertation argument Require short-term research access in New York City The call does not state that doctoral candidates must be enrolled at a U.S. university. International doctoral researchers are explicitly eligible. 2. College and University Faculty Faculty members may apply regardless of academic rank. This means eligibility is not restricted only to: Full professors Tenured professors Senior scholars Researchers at other academic ranks may also apply. This broad eligibility allows faculty members at different career stages to seek support for research projects in American history. 3. Independent Scholars Researchers who are not currently employed in a traditional university faculty position may also qualify as: Independent scholars This is particularly important because many research fellowships limit eligibility to scholars holding formal university appointments. The Gilder Lehrman programme explicitly recognizes independent scholarship as an eligible category. International Scholars Are Eligible The programme explicitly states that: International scholars are eligible to apply. There is therefore no requirement that applicants: Be U.S. citizens Be permanent residents of the United States Study at a U.S. university Hold an American academic appointment Applicants from universities, research institutions, and independent scholarly communities outside the United States may apply. However, successful Fellows must be able to conduct their research in New York City within the required period. Applicants should therefore consider immigration, travel, and logistical requirements when developing their project and anticipated budget. Research Must Be Conducted in New York City Successful Fellows are required to complete their research in: New York City The research must be completed within: One year of notification of the fellowship award This means applicants should already have a reasonably clear understanding of: Which archives they need Which collections they intend to consult Why those materials are necessary How much research time they expect to need How the $3,000 award will support the research visit The fellowship is therefore not simply a general award for producing scholarship from the applicant s home institution. It is specifically connected with a research trip to New York City. Primary Sources Are Central to the Application Applicants must include a list of the: Primary sources they expect to consult within their project proposal. This requirement is important because it helps the selection committee determine whether the proposed research trip is genuinely necessary and well planned. Candidates should therefore investigate collections before submitting their applications. A strong application should identify specific archival materials rather than saying only: “I plan to consult archives in New York.” Applicants should demonstrate that they know what materials exist and how those materials connect with their research questions. Fellowship Responsibilities Receiving the fellowship involves several responsibilities beyond conducting archival research. Successful Fellows must: Complete their research within one year of notification. Conduct their fellowship research in New York City. Meet with the Director of the Scholarly Fellowship Program during their research trip. Submit a written essay after the fellowship. Provide documentation regarding the archival collections consulted. These requirements ensure that the Fellowship contributes not only to the scholar s individual project but also to the Institute s broader scholarly mission. Meeting With the Fellowship Programme Director During their research trip to New York City, Fellows are required to meet with the: Director of the Scholarly Fellowship Program at the Gilder Lehrman Institute Applicants should therefore plan their research visit in coordination with the Institute. Post-Fellowship Essay Successful Fellows are required to submit an essay of: 750–1,000 words The essay should concern the Fellow s research topic. This creates an opportunity for Fellows to communicate aspects of their scholarship in an accessible format. Archival Collections Statement In addition to the essay, Fellows must provide: A separate paragraph documenting the archival collections consulted during the fellowship period. Researchers should therefore maintain a careful record of archives and collections used during their research trip. Application Requirements Applications require three major components: Project proposal Curriculum vitae Two recommendation letters Project Proposal Applicants must submit a project proposal of: 2–5 pages The proposal should include several specific elements. Current Contact Information Applicants should include current contact details as required by the application instructions. Project Description The proposal should explain: The research topic Central research question Historical significance Current stage of the research Scholarly contribution Why archival research is needed Primary Sources Applicants must list the primary sources they expect to consult. This should demonstrate preparation and feasibility. Anticipated Budget The proposal must also include an: Anticipated budget Applicants should explain how fellowship funds are likely to be used. Depending on the applicant s location and circumstances, this might include expenses associated with: Travel Accommodation Local transportation Research-related costs Candidates should develop a realistic rather than inflated budget. Curriculum Vitae Applicants must submit a: Curriculum vitae There is: No stated page limit The official call specifically says that the CV may be of any length. However, applicants should still present information clearly and professionally. Relevant sections may include: Academic education Doctoral research Academic appointments Publications Conference presentations Awards Fellowships Research experience Teaching Professional affiliations Public history work Two Letters of Recommendation Applicants must arrange: Two letters of recommendation The letters should come from: Established scholars Applicants should identify recommenders who understand both their research abilities and the importance of the proposed project. Strong recommenders may be able to comment on: Research originality Historical knowledge Archival competence Scholarly potential Feasibility of the project Importance of the research Candidates should contact recommenders well before the deadline. Application Deadline Applications must be submitted online by: 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on Monday, October 26, 2026 Applicants outside the United States should carefully convert the deadline into their local time zone. Submitting several days early can help avoid problems involving: Recommendation letters Uploads Application-system errors Time-zone confusion How to Apply Applications are submitted online through the Gilder Lehrman Institute fellowship portal. Official fellowship information APPLY HERE Contact Information Questions about the programme can be directed to: Email: fellowships@gilderlehrman.org Telephone: 646-366-9666, ext. 129 Candidates with eligibility or application questions should use the official contact information rather than relying solely on third-party fellowship listings. Examples of Current Fellows and Research Topics The range of projects supported by the programme demonstrates the breadth of American history scholarship considered eligible. Current Fellows include researchers working on subjects such as: Numbers and the formation of American political identity U.S. governance in the Panama Canal Zone The history of American civil litigation African American internationalism Slavery and violence in South Carolina Black midwives in early America Civil defense during the Cold War African American children during the Civil War Revolutionary-era political figures Women and urban economic life This diversity demonstrates that the programme supports work extending across: Early America Colonial history Nineteenth-century history African American history Legal history Diplomatic history Political history Social history Cold War history Applicants should therefore focus on the quality and archival foundation of their research rather than assuming that only highly traditional historical topics are competitive. Importance of Archival Preparation Because the fellowship supports short-term research rather than a long residential appointment, applicants should arrive with a clear archival plan. Before applying, candidates should identify: The specific collections they need Relevant documents Archive opening schedules Potential restrictions Research priorities Expected time needed A four-week research plan, for example, should identify what can realistically be accomplished during that period. A strong proposal demonstrates that the Fellowship will enable work that could not easily be completed without access to the relevant New York collections. Preparing a Competitive Project Proposal 1. Define a Clear Historical Question Avoid proposing a topic that is too broad. Instead of: “Slavery in America” a competitive research proposal should identify a focused problem, period, archive, population, or historical debate. 2. Explain the Scholarly Contribution Reviewers should understand what the project adds to existing knowledge. Applicants may explain whether their work: Challenges an existing interpretation Introduces new archival material Reframes a historical debate Connects previously separate literatures Examines an overlooked community 3. Identify Specific Primary Sources The application explicitly requires a list of primary sources. This is not a minor administrative detail. Applicants should demonstrate that they have already researched the collections relevant to their project. 4. Explain Why the Research Must Be Done in New York A strong application should establish why access to New York City collections is essential to the project. Reviewers should not be left wondering why the applicant needs to travel. 5. Create a Realistic Budget Because the fellowship provides $3,000, applicants should present a credible plan for how the funding will support their research. The budget should correspond to the scope and duration of the proposed visit. 6. Use the Special Priority Areas Strategically Applicants working on: Colonial America Slavery and abolition Cold War history should make that connection visible. The Institute explicitly states that these fields receive special attention in the current competition. Why the Gilder Lehrman Fellowship Can Be Valuable for PhD Candidates Doctoral researchers often need archival evidence that cannot be accessed remotely. A $3,000 fellowship can help reduce the financial barriers associated with research travel. For PhD candidates, this might support: Dissertation archival research Revising a chapter Expanding primary-source evidence Filling gaps before dissertation completion Developing material for publication The programme can also provide recognition from an established institution dedicated to American history. Why Faculty Researchers Should Consider Applying Faculty members at all ranks are eligible. A short research fellowship can be particularly useful for academics working on: A new book Article project Revision of a manuscript Archival expansion of an existing project New research agenda Because there is no rank restriction, both junior and senior faculty members can compete. Opportunities for Independent Scholars Independent scholars are also explicitly welcomed. Applicants outside formal university employment should ensure that their application demonstrates: Strong scholarly preparation Serious research experience Clear project objectives Appropriate archival methodology Potential contribution to American history Independent status does not itself make an applicant less eligible. Important Details at a Glance Organization: Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History Opportunity: Scholarly Fellowships Year: 2026 Number of awards: Ten Value: $3,000 each Research field: American history Eligible applicants: Doctoral candidates, college and university faculty at every rank, and independent scholars International applicants: Eligible Research location: New York City Research completion requirement: Within one year of award notification Project proposal: 2–5 pages CV: Any length References: Two letters from established scholars Post-fellowship essay: 750–1,000 words Deadline: October 26, 2026 at 11:59 p.m. ET Conclusion The Gilder Lehrman Scholarly Fellowships 2026 provide a valuable short-term research opportunity for scholars working across the broad field of American history. title: Terra.do Climate Fellowship 2026: Apply for the 12-Week Climate Change Learning for Action Programme
summary: Are you looking to build a career in climate action, deepen your understanding of climate change, or transition your existing professional skills into the rapidly growing climate sector? The Terra.do Climate Fellowship: Climate Change – Learning for Action offers a structured 12-week learning experience designed to help participants understand the complexities of climate change, explore practical solutions and identify where their skills can make the greatest contribution to climate action. The fellowship brings together a global community of climate professionals, researchers, entrepreneurs, advocates, educators, sustainability specialists, technologists and other professionals interested in addressing climate challenges. The programme combines expert-led learning, practical projects, discussions, mentorship, career development and networking to help participants move from understanding climate problems to taking meaningful action. According to Terra.do, the fellowship has supported more than 7,000 graduates across more than 96 countries, with an average course rating of 9.3 and a reported career transition rate of more than 60 percent. About the Terra.do Climate Fellowship The Climate Change: Learning for Action fellowship is an expert-guided programme focused on helping participants understand climate science, climate impacts, policy, economics, technology, finance, sustainability and practical climate solutions. The programme is designed around the idea that climate action requires people from different professional backgrounds and disciplines. Participants therefore have an opportunity to explore the connections between science, business, policy, technology, communications, finance, agriculture and social change. Terra.do describes the programme as a journey that helps participants understand the climate problem while identifying practical solutions and finding a meaningful role within the climate sector. Key Features of the Climate Fellowship The fellowship is delivered entirely online and is structured to accommodate professionals and other participants who may have existing work or personal commitments. Key programme features include 100% online learning. Approximately 6 to 10 hours of study and participation each week. Between 10 and 12 expert lectures. Weekly deep dives and discussion groups. Hands-on projects. Personalised feedback and support. Tailored career development support. A digital certificate upon graduation. The programme also provides access to more than 100 updated learning modules covering a broad range of climate-related subjects. What Will Participants Learn? The curriculum explores climate change from scientific, economic, political, technological, social and professional perspectives. Major subject areas include: Climate science – Understanding the scientific foundations of climate change and the processes driving global warming. Climate impacts—Examining local and global consequences of climate change and how warming affects ecosystems, societies and economies. Energy – Exploring energy systems and the transition towards cleaner and more sustainable energy. Food and agriculture – Understanding the relationship between climate change, food systems and agriculture. Carbon removal – Examining approaches to removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Climate politics—Exploring policy choices, governance and political approaches to climate action. Climate economics – Understanding the economic dimensions of climate change, including markets, costs and policy interventions. Climate communications – Learning how climate issues can be communicated effectively to different audiences. Climate finance – Exploring the role of financial systems and investment in addressing climate change. Climate risk – Understanding climate-related risks and their implications for organisations and communities. Corporate sustainability—Examining how organisations can incorporate climate considerations into business strategies. Adaptation – Exploring approaches for preparing communities and systems for the impacts of climate change. Alternative development models – Considering different approaches to economic and social development in the context of environmental sustainability. Expert-Led Climate Learning The fellowship brings together educators, scientists, entrepreneurs, lawyers, journalists, policy specialists and other practitioners working on climate solutions. The programme explains that climate action is shaped by multiple perspectives, including science, policy, technology and justice. Participants therefore have opportunities to learn from people actively working on climate challenges rather than relying exclusively on theoretical material. The programme has featured professionals such as clean-technology entrepreneur Danny Kennedy, climate scientist Dr. Zachary Labe, Stanford professor Mark Z. Jacobson and environmental lawyer Melissa Hornbein. Other experts highlighted by the programme include climate journalist David Roberts, Dr. Tracey Osborne, renewable-energy entrepreneur Dr. Jeremy Leggett, Jamie Alexander and Goldman Environmental Prize winner Kimiko Hirata. A Curriculum Designed for a Changing Climate Sector Climate science, technology, markets and policies are constantly evolving. The fellowship therefore states that its curriculum is regularly refreshed with new case studies, developments, tools and frameworks. Participants are exposed to current approaches and emerging developments designed to help them understand both the technical and human dimensions of climate solutions. This makes the programme relevant to professionals who want to understand not only the fundamentals of climate change but also how the climate sector is evolving. Climate Fellowship Syllabus and Weekly Structure The programme consists of 20 classes and more than 100 modules, supported by expert-led lectures and workshops, discussions, career support, networking and individual feedback. The syllabus begins with the fundamentals before progressing into more complex areas of climate solutions. Week 1: Introduction to Climate Change Participants begin by examining the fundamentals of climate change. Topics include: Building a simple climate model. The greenhouse effect. Radiative and climate forcing. Drivers of climate change. Week 2: Foundations of Climate Science The second week focuses on emissions and the global carbon cycle. Participants explore: The global carbon cycle. Global warming potential. Methane and other greenhouse gases. Emissions accounting. Week 3: Climate Impacts and Personal Resilience This stage examines the consequences of a changing climate, including: The significance of the 1.5°C target. When warming could stop. Changes in temperature and rainfall. Ice and sea-level changes. Ocean currents. The global carbon budget. Week 4: Climate Solutions and Communication Participants explore different approaches to addressing climate change and learn how to compare solutions based on factors such as impact and cost. The week also introduces mental models and different ways of framing climate issues. Week 5: Climate Economics, Politics and Justice The programme then examines the economic and political dimensions of climate change. Topics include: Climate change as a market failure. Alternative approaches to environmental economics. Climate policy options. Carbon pricing. Carbon markets. The social cost of carbon. Week 6: Systems Thinking and Energy Participants are introduced to systems thinking in relation to climate mitigation and the importance of energy. The programme includes an En-ROADS workshop by Climate Interactive , facilitated by a Climate Interactive ambassador. The supplied programme information displays the first six weeks of the syllabus in detail, while indicating that the wider curriculum continues beyond these modules. Weekly Learning Schedule The fellowship uses a combination of asynchronous learning, optional career sessions, expert deep dives, guest talks, live laboratories and networking activities. A typical week includes: Sunday: Asynchronous classes are released. Monday: Optional careers session. Tuesday: Optional deep-dive session. Wednesday: Guest talk. Thursday: Live laboratory. Friday: Optional networking and co-working session. The programme recognises that fellows may have work or family responsibilities. Mandatory sessions are recorded and can be watched asynchronously when participants are unable to attend live. Hands-On Projects and Practical Learning The fellowship goes beyond lectures by providing real-world assignments and projects. Participants work on individual and team projects designed to help them: Apply climate knowledge to their local context. Develop their climate voice. Build a portfolio of climate-related work. Strengthen communication skills. Improve collaboration skills. This practical component can be particularly useful for professionals who want to demonstrate their climate knowledge and experience when pursuing future opportunities. Personalised Feedback and Instruction Participants receive individualised support throughout the programme. The fellowship states that instructors track participants progress and provide the following: One-on-one support. Individual feedback on assignments. Personalised career-transition advice. Participants can also book one-on-one sessions to discuss their climate learning and career journey. Climate Lab Groups Participants meet weekly in small groups with instructors for interactive learning. These sessions include: Discussions around the week s topics. Presentations by fellow learners. Action-oriented and creative group activities. The group-based structure allows participants to learn from people with different professional backgrounds and perspectives. Career Development and Climate Job Support One of the central features of the fellowship is its focus on career development. Terra.do state that thousands of alumni have transitioned into roles across climate technology, policy, advocacy and other areas. Following completion of the programme, fellows can access a climate career coach who can help them: Determine how to enter the climate sector if they have limited previous experience. Identify climate jobs that match their existing skills. Develop a job-search strategy. Build a networking strategy. Accelerate their career transition. The programme therefore provides a pathway for participants who are not necessarily starting their careers in climate but want to transfer existing professional skills into the sector. Global Climate Mentorship Participants can also access guidance from experienced professionals working across different climate sectors. The programme highlights: More than 200 mentors. Mentors across more than 20 countries. Carefully curated climate experts. Mentorship across energy, policy, agriculture, sustainability, ESG, climate finance and other sectors. One-on-one time for personalised career guidance. This international mentorship component can help participants better understand career pathways and professional opportunities across the climate economy. Who Is the Climate Fellowship Designed For? The programme is not limited to one professional discipline. Instead, it is designed for people with different skills and backgrounds who want to contribute to climate solutions. Advocacy and Policy Professionals The fellowship is suitable for professionals interested in climate policy, adaptation, resilience, climate justice and strengthening climate-related work within government or non-governmental organisations. Business Professionals People working in sales, marketing, business development, finance and related functions can use the programme to explore climate career transitions or contribute to corporate climate leadership. Technologists Engineers, data scientists and product managers interested in climate technology, climate startups and technology-enabled climate solutions are also identified as potential participants. Climate Scientists Researchers, analysts and scientists working in academic, government or private-sector settings can use the programme to connect their expertise with real-world climate challenges. Sustainability Consultants Professionals working in sustainability consulting, corporate ESG strategy and environmental impact assessment can benefit from the programme s focus on systemic climate action. Community Organisers and Educators Grassroots activists, educators and nonprofit leaders working on public awareness, community mobilisation, climate justice and policy advocacy are also among the audiences identified by the programme. Global Eligibility and Geographic Reach The supplied programme information presents the fellowship as a global programme. Terra.do reports graduates from more than 96 countries, indicating a broad international community. However, the source does not provide a formal list of eligible nationalities, countries, races or continents, nor does it identify a race or ethnicity requirement. Prospective applicants should therefore consult the official application process for any eligibility conditions that may apply to the specific cohort. What Can Participants Gain From the Fellowship? The programme is structured to provide a combination of climate knowledge, practical experience, professional development and community. Key areas of value include: A structured understanding of climate science and climate solutions. Exposure to climate policy and economics. Knowledge of energy, agriculture, carbon removal and adaptation. Understanding of climate finance and climate risk. Practical project experience. Individual feedback from instructors. Career transition guidance. Access to climate mentors. Networking with an international community. Opportunities to learn from climate practitioners. A digital certificate upon graduation. Alumni Career Outcomes Terra.do highlights alumni who have moved into different climate-related roles and organisations. Examples provided on the programme page include transitions into executive assistance, programme management, commercial leadership, environmental project leadership, technical specialist positions and other climate-related roles. The programme also states that more than 200 fellows are now running climate startups across different sectors. In addition, more than 500 fellows are described as advancing climate and sustainability objectives within their organisations. Open House and Alumni Engagement Prospective applicants can also engage with alumni and instructors through open house sessions. These sessions provide opportunities to: Meet and interact with alumni. Learn more about the programme. Ask questions directly to instructors. Gain insights into the fellowship experience. Applicants who want more personalised guidance can also schedule a one-on-one discussion about the programme and potential climate career pathways. Fellowship Cost and Scholarship Information The listed course fee for the programme is US$1,990 . The programme states that applicants can pay the fee in instalments and that there is a three-week money-back guarantee for participants who are not satisfied within the specified period. The source also states that journalists may be eligible for scholarships of up to 80% , depending on their application. The supplied page also displays a scholarship invitation associated with the applicant s referral context. Prospective applicants should therefore check the application page to determine what scholarship or funding options are available to them. Application Process The stated application process is designed to be relatively straightforward. Step 1: Submit Your Application Applicants are asked to explain their motivation for joining the programme and can request scholarship support if they need financial assistance. Step 2: Admission and Scholarship Decision Terra.do states that applications are reviewed within 24 hours and that applicants are notified of admission and scholarship decisions. Step 3: Complete Payment and Enrol Successful applicants can pay the programme fee either in full or through instalments and secure their place in the upcoming cohort. Application Deadline and Cohort Start Date The application deadline is September 22 , while the upcoming cohort is scheduled to begin on September 28 . Applicants interested in joining the programme should submit their applications before the stated deadline and review the official application requirements before applying. How to Apply for the Terra.do Climate Fellowship Interested applicants can apply through the official Terra.do programme page. Before submitting an application, prospective fellows should carefully review the programme structure, syllabus, financial requirements, scholarship information and application conditions. APPLY HERE Why Consider the Climate Change: Learning for Action Fellowship? Climate change affects virtually every major sector of society, from energy and agriculture to finance, infrastructure, business, health, development and public policy. As organisations increasingly need professionals who understand climate risks and solutions, gaining structured knowledge of climate action can help professionals identify new areas where their existing skills can be applied. The Terra.do fellowship brings together scientific learning, practical projects, expert instruction, mentorship and career development within one programme. Its international community also gives participants an opportunity to learn alongside people approaching climate challenges from different professional and geographical perspectives. For professionals seeking to transition into climate work, researchers looking to connect their expertise with practical solutions, business professionals exploring climate leadership, or advocates and educators seeking stronger climate knowledge, the programme provides a structured environment for learning and professional development. Visit HERE for more information about the Terra.do Climate Fellowship 2026. Conclusion The Terra.do Climate Fellowship: Climate Change – Learning for Action is a 12-week online programme designed to help participants understand climate change and develop the knowledge, practical experience and professional connections needed to contribute to climate solutions. With more than 100 learning modules, expert-led lectures, weekly discussions, practical projects, personalised feedback, career support and access to an international network of climate professionals and mentors, the fellowship offers a multidisciplinary approach to climate education and career development. title: AARP Foundation California Quality Employment Grant 2026: Up to $750,000 for Projects Supporting Older Workers
summary: The AARP Foundation has announced a new grant opportunity aimed at improving access to quality employment for older adults with low incomes in California. Through its Request for Applications (RFA): Quality Employment for Older Workers in California , the Foundation intends to support projects that strengthen workforce systems, improve employment services, and create better pathways to stable and sustainable work for people aged 50 and above who experience financial insecurity. AARP Foundation plans to invest approximately $2 million in grant funding through this initiative and expects to support between four and eight organizations. Successful applicants may receive grants ranging from $250,000 to $750,000 , depending on the size, duration, activities, and expected outcomes of their proposed projects. The opportunity is particularly relevant to organizations, coalitions, workforce leaders, community organizations, and other eligible entities working to improve how workforce systems serve older workers. Rather than focusing primarily on conventional direct-service delivery, the RFA emphasizes systems change , age-inclusive workforce practices, improved coordination among services, and stronger pathways to quality employment. About the AARP Foundation California Quality Employment Grant The AARP Foundation is seeking innovative projects that can help make workforce systems more responsive to the needs of older adults with low incomes. Older workers can encounter significant challenges when seeking employment, remaining in work, changing careers, or re-entering the workforce after unemployment. These challenges can include age-related barriers in recruitment, limited access to relevant training, difficulty navigating employment and public-benefit systems, and a lack of coordinated support during periods of job transition. Through this funding opportunity, AARP Foundation wants to support approaches that address these structural and systemic challenges. The Foundation is particularly interested in projects that incorporate age-inclusive practices into workforce systems and services and create stronger pathways toward quality employment for adults aged 50 and above. What Does AARP Foundation Mean by Quality Employment? For this grant opportunity, quality employment goes beyond simply helping someone find a job. A quality job should provide conditions that allow an individual to achieve greater financial stability while developing the skills and support necessary to remain employed and progress professionally. According to the grant description, quality employment includes work that provides: Stable earnings. Fair and equitable treatment. Opportunities to develop skills. Opportunities for advancement. Flexibility that helps workers remain employed. Appropriate support during employment transitions. Conditions that contribute to longer-term employment sustainability. This means applicants should think beyond traditional job-placement activities. Strong proposals should demonstrate how their interventions can help improve the broader systems, structures, and services that determine whether older workers can access and maintain quality employment. Main Areas of Interest AARP Foundation has identified two major areas that applicants may address through their proposed projects. 1. Age-Inclusive Training, Education, and Employment Services The first area focuses on improving workforce training, education, and employment services so that they intentionally respond to the needs of older workers. Many existing workforce programs are designed for broad populations and may not adequately account for the circumstances faced by adults aged 50 and above. AARP Foundation is therefore interested in approaches that redesign or improve these programs to make them more age-inclusive. Potential activities may include: Redesigning job-connected training programs to intentionally serve older workers. Modifying workforce services to better address the needs of adults aged 50 and above. Developing new approaches for reaching older workers who may not be adequately served by existing employment systems. Creating recruitment strategies specifically designed to engage older workers. Helping older adults prepare for quality employment opportunities. Connecting older workers with employers offering suitable employment opportunities. Improving the ability of workforce organizations to identify and respond to barriers experienced by older job seekers. Developing employment pathways that recognize the experience, skills, and needs of older workers. Applicants should demonstrate how their proposed intervention could improve the effectiveness or inclusiveness of existing workforce systems rather than simply providing temporary assistance to individual participants. 2. Age-Inclusive Workforce Systems and Service Alignment The second major area of interest focuses on improving coordination among workforce systems, public agencies, community organizations, and other support services. Older adults experiencing unemployment or employment transitions may need to interact with multiple systems at the same time. These can include workforce development services, unemployment support, employment agencies, community organizations, and public-benefit programs. When these systems operate independently, individuals may encounter fragmented services, duplicated processes, unclear referral pathways, or difficulty understanding where to obtain appropriate support. AARP Foundation is therefore interested in projects that strengthen connections between these systems. Potential approaches could include: Building stronger connections between unemployment services and workforce development programs. Improving coordination between reemployment services and other employment-support systems. Developing stronger referral pathways between public agencies and community-based organizations. Testing coordinated service models specifically designed to reach older workers. Improving how older adults navigate multiple benefits and support services. Creating partnerships among organizations serving older adults experiencing employment transitions. Developing systems that make it easier for older workers to move between workforce and support services. Testing approaches that can eventually be replicated or adopted more broadly. The Grant Is Focused on Systems Change One of the most important aspects of this opportunity is that applicants should understand the distinction between systems change and traditional direct service delivery. AARP Foundation specifically states that projects should focus on systems change initiatives rather than direct service programs . This means an applicant should not simply propose to provide employment services directly to a group of older adults without explaining how the project will change, improve, coordinate, or strengthen the systems through which those services are delivered. For example, a conventional direct-service project might focus primarily on helping a specific number of individuals prepare résumés or find jobs. A systems-change project, by contrast, could examine how workforce organizations identify older job seekers, redesign their service models, improve referral systems, coordinate with community organizations, or change workforce practices so that older workers can consistently receive better support. Applicants should therefore clearly demonstrate the broader structural impact their project could have. Who Should Benefit From the Project? The proposed projects must primarily benefit older adults aged 50 and above with low incomes or financial insecurity . The target population is particularly important because the grant is designed around older workers who rely on employment to meet basic needs. Applicants should therefore demonstrate a clear understanding of the employment challenges faced by financially vulnerable older adults and explain how their proposed systems-level intervention will improve access to quality employment. A strong proposal should establish: Who the intended older-worker population is. What employment-related challenges this population experiences. Why existing systems and services are insufficient. What systemic barrier the project intends to address. How the proposed intervention will improve workforce systems. How the project will ultimately create better employment pathways. How success will be measured. Where Must Projects Be Implemented? The projects supported through this funding opportunity must be implemented in the state of California . This geographic requirement is central to the RFA. Applicants should ensure that their proposed activities, partnerships, workforce systems, and intended impact are connected to California. Organizations outside California should carefully review the complete RFA and FAQ before determining whether they are eligible to participate, particularly if they intend to partner with California-based organizations. The opportunity should not be interpreted as a general international or worldwide employment grant. Its stated purpose is to address quality employment for older adults with low incomes in California . How Much Funding Is Available? AARP Foundation expects to invest approximately $2 million through this grant opportunity. The Foundation anticipates making awards to up to four but no more than eight grantees . Individual grant awards are expected to range from: Minimum expected award: $250,000. Maximum expected award: $750,000. Applicants are expected to request an amount that is appropriate for the scope of their proposed project, activities, implementation period, and anticipated outcomes. The grant structure is designed to allow applicants to develop projects of different durations while matching their funding request to the scale of the intervention. Funding Based on Project Duration The maximum funding amount depends partly on the proposed implementation period. 12-Month Projects Projects proposed for a 12-month implementation period may request up to $375,000 . Applicants choosing this duration should ensure that the proposed activities and outcomes can realistically be achieved within one year. The project should have a clearly defined implementation strategy, measurable outcomes, and a realistic timeline demonstrating how the proposed systems change can occur during the funding period. 24-Month Projects Projects proposed for a 24-month implementation period may request up to $750,000 . A two-year project may provide greater opportunity to develop partnerships, test new approaches, implement systems changes, evaluate results, and refine interventions. However, a larger funding request should be supported by a clearly defined scope of work and a strong explanation of why the proposed activities require the requested level of investment. Important Proposal Considerations Organizations preparing an application should pay close attention to the central requirements of the RFA. Focus on Older Workers The proposed intervention must primarily affect adults aged 50 and above who have low incomes, experience financial insecurity, or depend on employment to meet basic needs. Demonstrate Systems-Level Impact The project should be designed to change or improve workforce systems rather than operate solely as a conventional direct-service program. Address Quality Employment Applicants should explain how their project will contribute to employment that offers stability, fair treatment, skill development, advancement opportunities, flexibility, and support. Establish California-Based Impact The project must be implemented in California, and the proposed activities should clearly demonstrate relevance to the state s workforce environment. Develop a Strong Partnership Strategy Because workforce systems involve multiple organizations and services, applicants should consider how collaboration, referrals, coordination, and service alignment can contribute to the proposed intervention. Connect Activities to Measurable Outcomes Applicants should explain what they intend to change and how they will determine whether the project has achieved its objectives. Rather than simply listing activities, the proposal should establish a logical connection between the identified problem, proposed intervention, expected outputs, and anticipated outcomes. Application Process The grant opportunity involves a two-stage application process . Stage One: Pre-Application Interested applicants must first submit a pre-application through AARP Foundation s grant portal. The pre-application is the initial screening stage of the funding process. Applicants should review the full RFA carefully before submitting their materials to ensure that the proposed project aligns with the Foundation s objectives, eligibility requirements, geographic restrictions, target population, and systems-change focus. The pre-application must be submitted through the AARP Foundation s Fluxx Grantee Portal . Stage Two: Full Application Following the review of pre-applications, selected applicants will be invited to submit a full application. According to the published schedule, invitations to submit full applications are expected around mid-September 2026 . The full application will provide shortlisted applicants with an opportunity to present their proposed project in greater detail. Organizations should therefore begin preparing their project concept, partnerships, implementation plan, expected outcomes, and budget before the invitation stage rather than waiting until the full application period begins. Key Dates and Deadlines Applicants should pay close attention to the following dates: Date Milestone August 6, 2026 Funding opportunity announced and pre-application made available Week of August 17, 2026 FAQ expected to become available September 1, 2026, at 7:00 p.m. PT / 10:00 p.m. ET Pre-application submission deadline Mid-September 2026 Selected applicants invited to submit full applications Mid-October 2026 Full application submission deadline October–November 2026 Clarification and follow-up period, as needed December 2026 Applicants notified of funding decisions Application Deadline The most immediate deadline is: September 1, 2026, at 7:00 p.m. Pacific Time / 10:00 p.m. Eastern Time. Applicants should avoid waiting until the final hours to submit their pre-application. Technical issues, incomplete information, or difficulties with the grant portal can create unnecessary risks close to the deadline. Where to Find the Full RFA The complete grant requirements, application instructions, eligibility information, and additional details are contained in AARP Foundation s official Request for Applications. Applicants should read the complete RFA rather than relying solely on summaries because the official document contains the detailed requirements governing the application. Questions and Technical Support Applicants who have questions about the RFA or require technical support with submitting an application through the AARP Foundation s Fluxx Grantee Portal can contact the AARP Foundation Grants Management team. Email: aarp_foundation_grants@aarp.org Questions relating to eligibility, proposal requirements, or technical submission issues should be addressed as early as possible so applicants have adequate time to resolve any concerns before the deadline. Frequently Asked Questions Can an individual apply for this grant? The opportunity is structured around projects led by eligible organizations, leaders, and coalitions rather than individual applicants seeking personal financial assistance. Potential applicants should consult the full RFA for the precise organizational eligibility requirements. Can organizations outside California apply? The RFA states that projects must be implemented in California . Organizations considering participation from outside the state should carefully review the full eligibility provisions and FAQ, particularly where partnerships with California-based organizations are involved. Can multiple organizations collaborate on a proposal? The RFA includes a question addressing proposals involving multiple partner organizations. Given the focus on workforce-system alignment, partnerships and collaboration may be particularly relevant to projects seeking to improve connections among public agencies, workforce organizations, community organizations, and support services. Applicants should consult the full RFA for the specific requirements governing collaborative proposals. What is the difference between quality employment and simply having a job? The grant opportunity takes a broader view of employment. Quality employment should provide stable earnings, fair treatment, opportunities for skills development and advancement, flexibility, and sufficient support to help workers sustain employment through subsequent transitions. Consequently, projects should demonstrate how their proposed systems changes can contribute to these broader employment outcomes. What does systems change mean in this opportunity? Systems change refers to interventions that alter or improve the way workforce systems, organizations, services, policies, processes, partnerships, or referral mechanisms operate. Applicants should therefore demonstrate how their project can produce changes that extend beyond providing temporary services directly to individual participants. How to Prepare a Competitive Application Organizations considering this opportunity can take several practical steps to strengthen their proposals. 1. Clearly Define the Problem Begin by identifying a specific workforce-system challenge affecting low-income older adults in California. Explain the problem using evidence, local knowledge, workforce data, organizational experience, or other credible information. 2. Identify the Systemic Barrier Do not stop at describing unemployment or financial insecurity. Explain why the existing workforce system is not adequately addressing the problem and identify the structural or organizational barrier that the project will address. 3. Demonstrate Age Inclusivity Explain how the proposed approach will intentionally address the circumstances and needs of workers aged 50 and above. The age-inclusive component should be central to the project rather than an incidental feature. 4. Build a Strong Theory of Change A strong proposal should demonstrate a logical progression: Problem → Systemic Barrier → Intervention → System Change → Improved Workforce Services → Better Employment Pathways → Improved Outcomes for Older Workers This makes it easier for reviewers to understand why the proposed project is likely to produce meaningful results. 5. Develop Meaningful Partnerships Consider which organizations influence the employment experiences of older workers. Potential partners could include workforce development organizations, public agencies, community organizations, employers, training institutions, and other relevant stakeholders. 6. Establish Measurable Outcomes Applicants should identify realistic indicators for determining whether the intervention is successful. Possible areas of measurement could include improvements in service coordination, referral effectiveness, workforce-system participation, employer engagement, access to training, or pathways to quality employment, depending on the proposed project. 7. Prepare a Realistic Budget The funding request should correspond with the scope and duration of the proposed intervention. A larger request should be supported by sufficient activities, staffing, partnerships, evaluation, and expected outcomes to justify the investment. 8. Review the Official RFA Carefully Finally, applicants should compare their proposed project against every requirement in the official RFA before submitting the pre-application. The official document should be treated as the authoritative source for eligibility and application requirements. At the same time, older workers bring substantial experience, professional knowledge, technical skills, institutional understanding, and other valuable capabilities to the workforce. The challenge is therefore not simply getting older adults into employment. It is also ensuring that workforce systems recognize their needs and help them access jobs that provide stability, fair treatment, development opportunities, flexibility, and sustainable employment conditions. The AARP Foundation grant provides an opportunity to address these challenges at a broader systems level. Instead of funding only individual employment interventions, the initiative seeks to encourage changes in the systems and services that shape how older workers access employment opportunities. Visit HERE to learn more about the AARP Foundation California Quality Employment Grant 2026. Final Takeaway The AARP Foundation Quality Employment for Older Workers in California Grant 2026 represents a significant funding opportunity for eligible organizations and coalitions seeking to improve workforce systems for financially vulnerable adults aged 50 and above. With approximately $2 million available , individual awards expected to range from $250,000 to $750,000 , and project periods of 12 to 24 months , the opportunity can provide substantial resources for organizations developing ambitious systems-change initiatives. However, applicants should pay particular attention to three fundamental requirements: the project must primarily benefit older adults aged 50+ with low incomes or financial insecurity , it must be implemented in California , and it must focus on systems change rather than primarily delivering direct services . The immediate deadline is September 1, 2026, at 7:00 p.m. Pacific Time / 10:00 p.m. Eastern Time for the pre-application.
