title: Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters Scholarships 2026–2027: Study Across Europe with Fully Funded Scholarship Opportunities
summary: The Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters (EMJM) programme offers an exceptional opportunity for students from around the world to pursue an international master s degree through a consortium of universities located in different countries. Unlike a conventional master s programme where students may remain at one university for the entire duration of their studies, Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are designed around international mobility. Students typically study at several universities and may also participate in research projects, traineeships, fieldwork, thesis preparation and other academic activities in different countries. The programme is supported by the European Union s Erasmus+ programme , and selected master s programmes can provide highly competitive scholarships to the best-ranked applicants worldwide. Depending on the individual programme, scholarships can contribute toward participation costs as well as travel, visa and living expenses. For students seeking an internationally recognised master s degree, exposure to different academic systems, multicultural learning environments and international professional networks, Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters can be one of the most valuable study opportunities available. Opportunity Category Scholarship / International Master s Degree Programme The Erasmus Mundus opportunity combines postgraduate study with competitive scholarship funding. Students apply to individual Erasmus Mundus Joint Master programmes rather than submitting one general application to Erasmus Mundus. What Are Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters? Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are prestigious international master s programmes that are jointly designed and delivered by a consortium of higher education institutions. A participating programme normally brings together at least three higher education institutions from at least three different countries . The consortium may also include associated partners from academic, research, professional, governmental, business or other non-academic sectors. This structure gives students the opportunity to experience higher education across different countries and institutions while completing one coordinated master s programme. Depending on the programme, students may move between participating universities during their studies. The exact mobility pathway varies from one master s programme to another, so prospective applicants should carefully examine the official programme website before applying. Why Study an Erasmus Mundus Joint Master? There are several reasons why Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are attractive to international students. 1. Study in multiple countries One of the defining characteristics of an Erasmus Mundus Joint Master is international mobility. Rather than completing the entire programme at one university, students may spend different parts of their master s degree at different institutions within the consortium. This can expose students to: Different European higher education systems International academic perspectives Multiple research environments Different cultures and languages International professional networks Diverse student communities Cross-border approaches to research and problem-solving The specific countries and universities involved depend on the master s programme selected. 2. International academic experience Erasmus Mundus programmes bring together students and academics from different parts of the world. Studying in such an environment can help students develop a broader understanding of their academic discipline while learning to work with people from different cultural and professional backgrounds. This can be particularly valuable for graduates interested in international development, public policy, communication, science, technology, environmental studies, business, social sciences and other disciplines where international collaboration is important. 3. Prestigious master s programmes Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are developed and delivered by international university consortia. The participating institutions work together to create an integrated programme rather than simply offering separate courses under a common name. Students therefore receive an academic experience built around collaboration between the participating institutions. 4. Opportunities for research and practical experience An Erasmus Mundus Joint Master is not necessarily limited to traditional classroom-based learning. Depending on the programme, students can undertake: Academic coursework Research activities Traineeships Practical projects Fieldwork Thesis preparation Master s thesis research Thesis defence The exact combination varies according to the selected programme. This makes it important for applicants to examine individual programme curricula before deciding which Erasmus Mundus master s programme best matches their academic and professional objectives. Erasmus Mundus Scholarships One of the most attractive features of the programme is the availability of competitive scholarships. Some Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters offer full scholarships to the best-ranked students worldwide . Scholarship arrangements vary according to the specific programme and the applicable funding rules. However, the official Erasmus Mundus information indicates that scholarships can cover or contribute toward major costs associated with participating in the master s programme. Potential areas of financial support include: Participation or programme costs Travel expenses Visa-related expenses Living allowance Because funding conditions can differ between programmes and application cycles, applicants should not assume that every Erasmus Mundus master s programme provides exactly the same scholarship package. The individual master s programme website should always be checked for the current scholarship amount, eligibility conditions, payment arrangements and covered expenses. How Long Are Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters? Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters generally last between one and two academic years . Programmes can comprise: 60 ECTS credits 90 ECTS credits 120 ECTS credits The duration depends on the specific master s programme. Applicants should therefore examine the programme description carefully to determine: Programme duration Number of semesters Required mobility periods Participating universities Study locations Internship or traineeship requirements Research requirements Thesis requirements Graduation arrangements What Degree Will You Receive? Students who successfully complete an Erasmus Mundus Joint Master may receive either a joint degree or multiple degrees , depending on the structure of the programme. Joint degree A joint degree is a single degree certificate issued on behalf of at least two higher education institutions within the consortium. Multiple degrees A multiple-degree arrangement means that the student receives at least two degree certificates from two higher education institutions belonging to the consortium. The precise degree arrangement is established by the individual Erasmus Mundus Joint Master. Students should therefore review the degree structure before applying and understand which institutions will award the qualification. Who Can Apply for Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters? Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are designed for students from around the world. The programme information states that students from all over the world are welcome to apply . Therefore, the opportunity is not restricted to applicants from European countries. Applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, the Caribbean, Oceania and other regions may be eligible, provided they satisfy the requirements of the particular master s programme they select. However, international eligibility does not mean that every applicant automatically qualifies for every programme. Each Erasmus Mundus master s programme establishes its own academic and admission requirements. Academic Requirements The general requirement is that applicants must: Hold a bachelor s degree or first degree ; or Be in the final year of their bachelor s degree and graduate before the master s programme begins. Applicants may also qualify if they can demonstrate an equivalent level of learning. Where an equivalent qualification is used, it must be officially recognised in accordance with the relevant national legislation and practices of the country where the degree is awarded. This means prospective applicants should carefully verify whether their existing qualification is considered equivalent to a bachelor s degree for their selected Erasmus Mundus programme. Final-Year Bachelor s Students Students who have not yet completed their bachelor s degree may still be able to apply. However, applicants in their final year must graduate before the Erasmus Mundus Joint Master begins. This is particularly important because applicants should not assume that being accepted while completing a bachelor s degree means they can postpone graduation indefinitely. Students should check the individual master s programme for its specific documentation and graduation verification requirements. Eligibility for Applicants from Africa Students from African countries can apply to Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters. There is no general restriction limiting the opportunity to European applicants. Applicants from African countries can compete for available places and scholarships alongside eligible applicants from other parts of the world. For example, prospective applicants from countries such as: Kenya Uganda Tanzania Rwanda Ethiopia Ghana Nigeria South Africa Zambia Zimbabwe Malawi Botswana Namibia Senegal Cameroon Egypt Morocco Other African countries may explore the available catalogue and determine whether they meet the admission requirements of individual programmes. Nationality alone, however, does not guarantee admission or a scholarship. Academic qualifications and programme-specific eligibility requirements remain important. Application Process One of the most important things prospective applicants should understand is that there is not one universal application form for all Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters . Students apply directly to the institution or consortium running their chosen programme . The application process can therefore differ significantly from one master s programme to another. Step 1: Search the Erasmus Mundus catalogue The first step is to explore the official Erasmus Mundus catalogue and identify master s programmes relevant to your academic background and career objectives. When searching the catalogue, applicants should pay attention to: Programme title Academic discipline Participating universities Participating countries Programme duration Mobility requirements Admission requirements Application deadline Scholarship availability Required documents Language requirements Step 2: Visit the master s programme website After identifying an interesting programme, applicants should visit its official programme website. The programme website is the authoritative source for the specific admission requirements and application instructions. Applicants should not rely solely on general Erasmus Mundus information because individual master s programmes can have different requirements. Step 3: Check the academic requirements Applicants should determine whether their bachelor s degree or equivalent qualification is accepted. They should also review any programme-specific requirements relating to: Academic discipline Previous coursework Grade requirements Professional experience Language proficiency Research experience Technical skills Other qualifications Step 4: Check scholarship requirements If funding is important to you, determine whether the programme offers Erasmus Mundus scholarships and whether you need to complete any additional scholarship-related section of the application. Some programmes may assess applicants for scholarships as part of the main application process, while others may provide specific instructions. Step 5: Prepare the required documents The exact documents vary by programme, but applicants should expect to provide some combination of: Bachelor s degree certificate Academic transcripts Proof of graduation or expected graduation Curriculum vitae Motivation letter Proof of language proficiency, where required Identification documents Recommendation letters, where required Other programme-specific supporting documents Applicants should follow the official programme instructions carefully because submitting an incomplete application can affect eligibility. Step 6: Submit before the programme deadline Once the application is complete, submit it through the application system specified by the master s programme. Do not assume that there is one universal Erasmus Mundus deadline. The deadline is determined by the individual programme. When Is the Erasmus Mundus Application Deadline? There is no single universal deadline for all Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters . The official Erasmus Mundus information states that, in most cases, applications should be submitted between October and January for programmes beginning during the following academic year. However, the exact deadline depends on the master s programme. Applicants should therefore check the official website of their selected programme for the precise application deadline. Important deadline advice Because many programmes have competitive scholarship selection processes, prospective students should begin preparing well before October. Waiting until the final days of an application period can create problems if you need: Academic transcripts Recommendation letters Language test results Certified documents Passport or identification documents A strong motivation statement Additional programme-specific documentation Deadline: Generally October to January for programmes starting in the following academic year, but the exact deadline varies by master s programme. What Makes the Scholarship Competitive? Erasmus Mundus scholarships are highly competitive because they are intended for the best-ranked applicants. Applicants therefore need to do more than simply meet the minimum admission requirements. A strong application should demonstrate a clear connection between the applicant s: Academic background Professional or extracurricular experience Motivation for the chosen programme Career objectives Relevant skills Interest in the programme s academic focus International or cross-cultural interests Potential contribution to the programme community How to Strengthen Your Application Research the programme carefully Do not apply simply because a programme offers a scholarship. Read the curriculum, mobility structure, research areas, participating universities and career outcomes. Your motivation statement should demonstrate that you understand what the programme offers. Match your background to the programme Applicants should clearly explain how their previous academic and professional experiences prepare them for the master s programme. For example, if your bachelor s degree is in communication, you should identify relevant communication, research, media, digital, development, public relations or related experience when applying to an appropriate programme. Build a strong motivation statement A strong motivation statement should explain: Why you want to study the programme Why the subject is important to you Why you selected that particular Erasmus Mundus programme What experience you bring What you hope to learn How the programme fits your career plans What you intend to contribute after graduation Avoid writing a generic statement that could be submitted to any university. Demonstrate international motivation Because Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are inherently international, applicants should demonstrate their ability and willingness to learn and collaborate in multicultural environments. International exposure can come from education, work, volunteering, research, community projects or other relevant experiences. Start early Applicants should begin preparing months before the deadline. A useful preparation timeline could include: Several months before applications open Research programmes Compare academic requirements Identify suitable programmes Review scholarship conditions Before the application deadline Prepare your CV Draft your motivation letter Request recommendation letters Obtain academic documents Check language requirements Prepare any required tests Before submission Review every requirement Check document formats Proofread the application Confirm the correct application portal Submit before the deadline Advice and Support for Applicants Prospective applicants can also find resources through the Erasmus Mundus Association , which provides information and resources intended to help applicants understand the programmes and application process. These resources can include programme contacts, events involving national volunteer representatives and stories from successful applicants. Learning from previous applicants can help prospective students better understand the application process and prepare a stronger submission. No Application date yet. In most cases, you should submit your application between October and January for courses starting the following academic year. Erasmus Mundus in Numbers The Erasmus Mundus programme has a substantial international track record. According to the official Erasmus+ information referenced by the programme, almost 50,000 students have participated since 2004 . This long history demonstrates the scale and international reach of Erasmus Mundus and highlights the programme s role in facilitating international postgraduate education. Erasmus Mundus Opportunities Beyond Students Although this opportunity is focused on students seeking master s degrees, Erasmus+ also provides other forms of support. Grants for higher education institutions Erasmus+ provides grants to higher education institutions to develop and run Erasmus Mundus Joint Master programmes. Institutions interested in participating should consult the official Erasmus+ information for organisations. Opportunities for researchers Researchers may also find related opportunities under the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions , including postdoctoral fellowships and staff exchanges. Other Erasmus+ opportunities Erasmus+ also provides various opportunities and forms of support for students, staff and other eligible participants. Frequently Asked Questions Is Erasmus Mundus available to students from Africa? Yes. Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters welcome applications from students around the world. African students can apply provided they meet the requirements of the particular master s programme. Do I need to already have a master s degree? No. The general requirement is a bachelor s degree or equivalent first degree. Students in the final year of their bachelor s degree may also apply, provided they graduate before the master s programme begins. Can final-year undergraduate students apply? Yes. Final-year bachelor s students can apply, but they must complete and graduate from their bachelor s programme before the Erasmus Mundus master s programme begins. Are Erasmus Mundus scholarships fully funded? Some Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters offer full scholarships to the best-ranked students worldwide. Scholarship coverage can include participation costs and contributions toward travel, visa and living expenses. The exact funding package varies by programme. Can I choose any university in Europe? No. Applicants apply to specific Erasmus Mundus Joint Master programmes, each of which has its own consortium of participating universities. Students follow the mobility structure established by their chosen programme. How many universities participate in an Erasmus Mundus Joint Master? An Erasmus Mundus Joint Master normally involves at least three higher education institutions from at least three different countries, together with associated partners. How long does an Erasmus Mundus master s degree take? The programmes generally last between one and two academic years and may comprise 60, 90 or 120 ECTS credits. Will I receive one degree or several degrees? Depending on the programme, you may receive either a joint degree issued on behalf of multiple institutions or multiple degrees issued by two or more institutions in the consortium. Is there one Erasmus Mundus application deadline? No. Each master s programme establishes its own deadline. In most cases, applications are submitted between October and January for programmes beginning in the following academic year. Where do I apply? You apply directly to the institution or consortium running the Erasmus Mundus Joint Master programme you have selected. Where can I find available programmes? You can search the official Erasmus Mundus catalogue for the latest programmes available. Conclusion The Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters programme represents a major opportunity for international students seeking an advanced degree in a highly international academic environment. With master s programmes delivered by consortia of universities across different countries, students can gain international academic exposure, participate in research and practical activities, build cross-cultural networks and potentially earn a joint or multiple-degree qualification. The availability of competitive scholarships makes the opportunity particularly attractive to students who may otherwise find international postgraduate study financially difficult. Selected scholarship recipients can receive support toward participation costs as well as travel, visa and living expenses, depending on the individual programme. However, prospective applicants should remember that Erasmus Mundus is not a single master s course with one universal application deadline. The programme consists of numerous individual Joint Masters, each with its own participating universities, academic focus, admission criteria, scholarship arrangements and application deadline. The best strategy is therefore to begin early, search the official Erasmus Mundus catalogue, identify programmes that match your academic and career goals, study the individual programme requirements carefully and submit a well-prepared application directly through the appropriate programme. title: We Are Not Waiting 2026: Young Changemakers Aged 14–35 Invited to Submit Abstracts for Global Youth-Led Systems Change Anthology
summary: We Are Not Waiting is a global youth-led initiative inviting young people who are already creating fairer, more sustainable and socially just futures to put their work on the record through an open-access anthology co-produced by The 50 Percent at the Club of Rome and the UNESCO–MOST BRIDGES UK Hub . The initiative is calling on young practitioners aged 14 to 35 who are actively working to transform communities and systems through areas such as regenerative economics, climate justice, circular living, peacebuilding, mutual aid, art, culture and storytelling. Rather than focusing only on theories about what a better future could look like, We Are Not Waiting seeks to document what young people are already doing in practice. Across communities worldwide, young people are organising, restoring ecosystems, developing alternative economic models, creating networks of solidarity, strengthening social cohesion, using creativity to challenge dominant narratives and finding new approaches to persistent social and environmental problems. Applicants do not need to be academics, professional researchers or established writers. The organisers are specifically interested in lived experience, practical action and original perspectives from young people who are actively engaged in the work they want to write about. Interested participants must submit an abstract of no more than 500 words by 31 August 2026 . Approximately 18 contributions are expected to form the final anthology. Applicants whose abstracts are selected will be invited to develop their ideas into full contributions of approximately 2,000 words , with editorial support provided throughout the writing process. The resulting open-access anthology will contain six chapters covering six major themes of systems change , with the project aiming to launch the publication at the UNESCO MOST Forum 2027 . About the We Are Not Waiting Initiative We Are Not Waiting : Amplifying Youth-Led Initiatives for Systems Change is designed around a simple but important idea: young people are not merely waiting for governments, institutions or established leaders to create solutions to the world s interconnected challenges. They are already building alternatives. The project centres young people aged 14–35 as designers and practitioners of alternative systems that are already in motion. It aims to showcase real-world initiatives and create a durable record of how youth-led systems change is happening in communities. The initiative has two major components: An open-access anthology comprising six chapters across six themes, with the aim of launching at the UNESCO MOST Forum 2027. A webinar series exploring the six themes through one question-and-answer session and two youth-led thematic sessions. At the heart of the project is the anthology, which is intended to be much more than a traditional collection of essays. It will serve as a policy-relevant record of youth-led systems change grounded in practical experiences. What Makes the We Are Not Waiting Anthology Different? The anthology is being deliberately designed to place young people s knowledge, experiences and perspectives at its centre. Three characteristics distinguish the publication: It is written, reviewed and edited by young people themselves. It is grounded in real-world practice rather than abstract discussion alone. It will be published in an open-access format , making the resulting knowledge accessible to a wider audience. The project provides young practitioners with an opportunity to document what they have learned through their initiatives while contributing to broader conversations about systemic change, social transformation and innovation. Who Can Submit an Abstract? The call is open to anyone aged 14 to 35 at the time of submission who is actively engaged in work connected to at least one of the anthology s six themes. Applicants do not need: Academic credentials; An institutional affiliation; To be professional researchers; To be established writers; or To have definitive solutions to the challenges they are addressing. Instead, the central requirement is that the proposed contribution must be grounded in genuine lived experience and real engagement with the issue or initiative being discussed . Applicants may submit either: Individually , or As part of a small team . For team submissions, all contributing authors must satisfy the 14–35 age requirement . The organisers particularly encourage contributions from the Global Majority and indigenous communities , helping ensure that perspectives and knowledge systems that may be underrepresented in conventional academic and policy discussions are included. Special Submission Requirement for Applicants Aged 18 and Under There is an additional submission procedure for younger participants. If an entrant is 18 years old or younger , their submission must be made on their behalf by an adult, such as: A parent; A guardian; or A teacher. The submission should include the young entrant s details together with the adult s contact information. This does not change the emphasis on the young person s ideas and experience; it is a procedural requirement for submitting the application. What Should You Submit? Applicants are invited to submit an abstract of no more than 500 words . The abstract should be written in the applicant s own voice using clear and accessible language. Academic or highly technical terminology is not required. The organisers want submissions that communicate real experiences and original thinking rather than attempting to sound like conventional academic papers. A strong abstract should address four key areas . 1. Describe Your Initiative, Project or Practice Explain the initiative, project, activity, network or practice that you want to write about. Applicants should provide enough context for reviewers to understand: What the work involves; Where or within what context it operates; What issue it seeks to address; Who is involved; and What the applicant s connection to the initiative is. 2. Explain What Makes the Work Distinct Applicants should explain what their work does differently. Consider questions such as: What conventional approach does the initiative challenge? What does the work refuse or seek to change? What alternative does it provide? How does the initiative rethink an existing system or practice? The objective is to demonstrate how the work contributes to creating or imagining different systems rather than merely reproducing existing approaches. 3. Ground the Contribution in Concrete Examples The anthology is focused on practice. Applicants should therefore show that their proposed full contribution will include real examples rather than relying exclusively on theoretical arguments. This could include experiences from communities, projects, campaigns, organisations, networks, cultural initiatives, environmental actions or other practical work. 4. Reflect on Learning and Broader Systems Change Applicants should also explain what they and their communities have learned through the work. The abstract should indicate how the initiative has contributed, or could contribute, to broader systemic change. The focus is therefore not simply on describing an activity but on examining what that activity reveals about how systems can be challenged, repaired, redesigned or transformed. Six Themes for the We Are Not Waiting Anthology Applicants must connect their abstract to one of six major themes. Theme 1: Re-weaving the Future — Networks and Economies That Make the World Anew This theme focuses on regenerative economics and community-centred alternatives to conventional economic systems. The organisers are interested in projects and practices demonstrating how young people are redesigning systems involving: Exchange; Value creation; Resource sharing; Community economies; Regenerative approaches; and Networks built around relationships and collective wellbeing. The emphasis is on a relational rather than merely technical approach to economic transformation. Young people who are experimenting with alternative economic systems, community-led resource models or regenerative approaches may find this theme particularly relevant. Theme 2: Building Resilience Through Ecological Resistance and Restoration This theme centres on climate justice, ecological resistance and environmental restoration . The organisers are seeking stories and experiences that demonstrate how young people are defending, restoring and renewing the living world. Relevant work may involve areas such as: Climate justice activism; Ecosystem restoration; Community environmental action; Ecological resistance; Biodiversity protection; Environmental justice; and Relationships between communities and ecosystems. The focus extends beyond simply managing environmental problems. Contributors are encouraged to reflect on what it means to actively defend and renew the living world . Theme 3: Living Circular Futures — Small Changes, Big Difference The third theme explores circular living and low-impact innovation . The organisers are particularly interested in concrete and practice-oriented examples showing how people can adapt their ways of living, producing, consuming and sharing resources. Contributions may explore change occurring at different levels, including: Personal practices; Community initiatives; Local innovation; Circular economic models; Low-impact approaches; and Broader systemic transformation. Applicants should demonstrate what circularity looks like when translated from an idea into real-world practice. Theme 4: Between Fracture and Repair — Youth-Led Peacebuilding and Social Cohesion This theme examines the role young people play in peacebuilding and strengthening social cohesion . It recognises that peace has both political and deeply personal dimensions. Contributions may explore experiences involving: Youth-led peacebuilding; Community reconciliation; Social cohesion; Repairing fractured relationships; Conflict transformation; Freedom; and Everyday practices that contribute to peace. The organisers welcome work that examines both large-scale political realities and the everyday experiences through which fractured communities seek repair. Theme 5: Communities of Care — Youth-Led Networks Built on Solidarity, Not Charity The fifth theme focuses on mutual aid and community solidarity . The anthology seeks contributions that demonstrate the distinction between mutual aid and conventional charitable giving. The central editorial perspective is community over individuality . Applicants could examine how young people are developing structures and networks of care that: Prioritise solidarity; Strengthen communities; Share resources; Support collective wellbeing; Build reciprocal relationships; and Avoid reproducing dependency. This theme is particularly relevant to young people working within community networks and grassroots initiatives where care is understood as a collective responsibility. Theme 6: Stories That Move Systems — Art, Culture and Storytelling as Tools for Transformation The final theme explores the role of art, culture, narrative and storytelling in systems change . The organisers are seeking contributions showing how creative practices can actively shape transformation rather than simply illustrate social issues. Relevant work could involve: Visual art; Cultural practice; Storytelling; Film; Performance; Literature; Community narratives; Creative campaigns; and Other forms of cultural expression. Applicants should demonstrate how creative practice or storytelling functions as an instrument for changing systems, perspectives, narratives or relationships. What Happens If Your Abstract Is Selected? Successful applicants will move from the abstract stage into development of the full anthology. Selected authors will be invited to prepare a contribution of approximately 2,000 words . Importantly, authors will not be expected to navigate the development process alone. The project s editorial team will provide editorial support throughout the process , helping contributors develop their initial abstracts into full pieces suitable for publication. This support is particularly significant because applicants do not need previous academic publishing or professional writing experience. The intention is to enable practitioners with valuable lived experience to communicate what they have learned in a clear and accessible way. Approximately 18 Contributions Will Be Featured The anthology is expected to bring together approximately 18 contributions from young practitioners. These contributions will collectively cover the six themes and document different approaches to youth-led systems change. By bringing these experiences together in one open-access publication, the project seeks to create a record that can contribute to discussions among young people, communities, researchers, institutions, practitioners and policymakers. Planned Launch at UNESCO MOST Forum 2027 The project aims to launch the completed six-chapter anthology at the UNESCO MOST Forum 2027 . This gives selected contributors an opportunity for their experiences and perspectives to become part of a publication intended to contribute to wider conversations about social transformation and systems change. The open-access format will also help make the anthology available beyond conventional academic or institutional audiences. Important Guidance on Artificial Intelligence and LLM Use Applicants should pay close attention to the project s guidelines concerning artificial intelligence and large language models. The organisers strongly emphasise that the call is designed to uncover original thinking, creativity and authentic perspectives from young practitioners . For this reason, using AI language models to draft, substantially revise or generate sections of a submission is not advised . The organisers explain that they expect to receive a large volume of submissions. Although AI-detection tools are imperfect, editors may recognise recurring patterns in language, tone and ideas that can cause an otherwise strong submission to appear less original or inspired. According to the guidelines, submissions that appear to rely heavily on AI are therefore likely to receive a lower assessment than work produced without such use. Limited AI Uses That Are Permitted AI tools may be used for limited supporting purposes, including: Checking grammar and spelling; Formatting references; Translating source material from languages other than English; and Conducting initial literature searches, provided the information is subsequently independently verified. Applicants who use AI in their contribution are required to include an AI declaration . The declaration must identify: The AI model and version used; The purpose or purposes for which it was used; and Confirmation that relevant data and references have been independently checked and verified by the author or authors. Applicants should therefore ensure that the ideas, experiences, arguments and core writing in their submission genuinely represent their own perspective. Why Young Practitioners Should Consider This Opportunity We Are Not Waiting offers young changemakers an avenue to turn practical experience into a documented contribution to wider conversations about systems change. For young people already engaged in community organising, environmental restoration, alternative economic practices, peacebuilding, mutual aid, cultural work or other transformative initiatives, the anthology provides an opportunity to: Document lessons from practical experience; Share approaches that may be useful to other communities; Contribute original youth perspectives to systems-change discussions; Develop a full written contribution with editorial support; Become part of an open-access publication; Connect practical grassroots experience with wider policy and systems-change conversations; and Help demonstrate that young people are already creating alternatives rather than simply waiting for future solutions. The call is particularly accessible because applicants do not need formal academic credentials, professional writing experience or institutional affiliations. The We Are Not Waiting Webinar Series Alongside the anthology, the initiative has hosted a webinar series highlighting youth-led projects already modelling ethical, ecological and socially just futures. Each session has been grounded in practical action and hosted, moderated and shaped by young people. The webinar programme includes: We Are Not Waiting: Q A Webinar Building New Systems: From Regenerative Economies to Climate Justice and Circular Living The Human Side of Systems Change: Peacebuilding, Mutual Aid and Cultural Transformation Prospective applicants can use these sessions, together with the project s Q A guide, to gain a clearer understanding of the themes, process and type of contributions being sought. About The 50 Percent at the Club of Rome The 50 Percent at the Club of Rome works to position youth leadership at the centre of systems change. Its work supports and amplifies young people who are already developing and implementing transitions that established institutions may still be discussing or debating. Within We Are Not Waiting, this philosophy is reflected in the emphasis on treating young people not simply as beneficiaries or future leaders, but as active designers and practitioners of systems change in the present. About the UNESCO–MOST BRIDGES UK Hub The UNESCO–MOST BRIDGES UK Hub generates humanities-informed research from the ground up. Its approach works with inclusive knowledge systems to support social transformation and contribute to policy and practice. Through the collaboration with The 50 Percent, the initiative seeks to connect practical youth-led knowledge and lived experience with broader research, policy and systems-change discussions. How to Submit an Abstract Applicants should first carefully review the programme information and Q A guidance before preparing their abstract. The submission process can be approached as follows: Confirm that you are aged 14–35 at the time of submission. Identify which of the six themes most closely relates to your work. Choose a real initiative, project or practice in which you are genuinely engaged. Prepare an abstract of no more than 500 words . Explain the initiative and its context. Describe what makes the work different from existing approaches. Show how the proposed contribution will use concrete examples. Reflect on what you and your community have learned and how the work relates to broader systems change. Write in your own clear and accessible voice. Review the project s AI guidelines carefully. If AI has been used within the permitted parameters, include the required AI declaration. Submit the abstract through the official submission form before the deadline. Applicants aged 18 or under should remember that an adult, such as a parent, guardian or teacher, must make the submission on their behalf and provide the required contact details. Official programme information: https://the50percent.org/programmes/we-are-not-waiting/ Submit your abstract: https://airtable.com/appsPZlhB6lztA78J/pagdYt0xmDeMv4O85/form Q A guide: https://the50percent.org/news/we-are-not-waiting-a-qa-guide-to-the-youth-led-systems-change-anthology/ Application Deadline The deadline to submit an abstract for the We Are Not Waiting youth-led systems change anthology is 31 August 2026 . Interested young practitioners should allow sufficient time to prepare an original abstract of no more than 500 words, ensure it addresses the required areas and complete the submission process before the deadline. Conclusion The We Are Not Waiting 2026 call for abstracts is an opportunity for young people who are already creating change to document their experiences and bring practical youth-led solutions into wider conversations about the future of societies, economies, communities and ecosystems. Instead of asking applicants to speculate about what young people might accomplish someday, the initiative focuses on what they are already building today . Whether that work involves regenerating ecosystems, developing community-centred economies, experimenting with circular living, repairing social divisions, building networks of mutual aid or using art and storytelling to transform narratives, the anthology seeks contributions grounded in action and lived experience. With no requirement for academic credentials, institutional affiliation or professional writing experience, the call creates space for young practitioners whose knowledge has emerged directly from doing the work. Selected applicants will have the opportunity to transform their initial abstracts into approximately 2,000-word contributions with editorial support and potentially have their experiences documented in an open-access anthology planned for launch at the UNESCO MOST Forum 2027. Young changemakers aged 14–35 who are actively working within one of the six themes should review the official guidance, prepare a clear and original abstract in their own voice, and submit their work by 31 August 2026 . title: University of Cambridge DE-GSJ Free Online Courses 2026: Apply for Fully Funded Sustainability, Climate and International Law Training
summary: Applications are open for the 2026 Fall Courses under the Democratising Education for Global Sustainability and Justice (DE-GSJ) Programme , an international educational initiative co-hosted by Lucy Cavendish College and Hughes Hall at the University of Cambridge . The programme provides learners around the world with free access to specialised education focused on sustainability, international law, public policy, climate change, biodiversity and sustainable development. For the 2026 Fall offering, applicants can express interest in courses addressing the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), and the Paris Agreement . The Fall courses will run between September and November 2026, with the full application deadline set for 1 September 2026 at 11:59 PM BST . The DE-GSJ Programme is particularly valuable for law and policy leaders, government officials, academics, civil society professionals, practitioners and other individuals interested in using law and policy to address some of the world s most pressing sustainability and justice challenges. About the Democratising Education for Global Sustainability and Justice Programme The Democratising Education for Global Sustainability and Justice (DE-GSJ) Programme was created to harness the potential of international law to empower governments and communities around the world, with particular attention to highly vulnerable countries facing interconnected global crises. Co-hosted by Lucy Cavendish College and Hughes Hall at the University of Cambridge , the initiative makes education concerning the law and policy dimensions of sustainability more accessible to learners internationally. The programme also seeks to train law and policy specialists who can contribute to implementing essential international treaties at different levels of governance. Rather than approaching sustainability solely as an environmental issue, the programme explores the important relationship between sustainable development, international agreements, governance, public policy and legal frameworks. This gives participants an opportunity to understand not only major global sustainability challenges, but also how laws, treaties, institutions and policies can be used to translate international commitments into practical action. 2026 DE-GSJ Fall Courses The DE-GSJ educational offerings page states that applications are open for its Fall Courses 2026 . Three courses are included in the Fall 2026 schedule: Key Essentials: The Sustainable Development Goals and the Law Course dates: 28 September – 9 October 2026 Key Essentials: Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), Sustainable Development and the Law Course dates: 12 October – 23 October 2026 Key Essentials: The Paris Agreement, Sustainable Development and the Law Course dates: 26 October – 6 November 2026 These dates allow learners to potentially build knowledge across several interconnected areas of international sustainability law during the Fall 2026 period. 1. Key Essentials: The Sustainable Development Goals and the Law The Key Essentials: The Sustainable Development Goals and the Law course provides an introduction to emerging approaches and frameworks in sustainable development law. It is designed for leaders and learners involved in areas such as: Law; Policymaking; Policy analysis; Legal and policy practice; Monitoring and reporting; Government; Academia; Civil society; and Practitioner communities. The course examines important challenges and possible solutions relating to sustainable development and considers the role that law can play in scaling up implementation globally and within learners own jurisdictions. Learning Objectives Through the course, learners are introduced to the relevance of sustainable development law and governance. Participants are encouraged to: Understand the relevance of sustainable development law and governance; Think critically about how sustainable development is reflected in legal and governance systems worldwide; Understand the role of governance within sustainable development law; Strengthen the role of law and policy in monitoring and reporting; and Explore opportunities to advance careers related to global sustainability and justice. Course Modules The Sustainable Development Goals and the Law course covers: Module 1: Introduction to the SDGs Module 2: Sustainable Development Law Principles and Practices Module 3: Law and Practice of SDGs in the Global Economy Module 4: Law and Practice of SDGs in the Global Biosphere Module 5: Law and Practice of SDGs Module 6: Course Conclusion and Final Remarks 2. Key Essentials: Convention on Biological Diversity, Sustainable Development and the Law The second Fall 2026 course focuses on biodiversity and the international legal frameworks designed to protect it. The programme highlights the seriousness of global biodiversity loss and provides learners with an overview of the Global Biodiversity Framework under the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity . It examines challenges, possible solutions and the role of law in strengthening implementation internationally and within individual jurisdictions. Learning Objectives Participants will have the opportunity to: Examine major biodiversity law and governance challenges; Explore the Global Biodiversity Framework; Understand tools available to policymakers and lawmakers, including those relating to finance, transparency and science; Identify and analyse innovative domestic legal and policy solutions; Strengthen understanding of monitoring and reporting through law and policy; and Develop knowledge relevant to careers in sustainability and justice. What Does the Biodiversity Course Cover? The course begins with an introduction to its structure and resources and includes engagement with instructors and learners from different parts of the world. Participants are introduced to the Convention on Biological Diversity , COP15 developments and the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework . The subsequent modules explore several major areas. Nature Conservation, Ecosystem Restoration and Biodiversity Protection Learners examine international goals and targets related to reducing threats to biodiversity, slowing extinction, maintaining genetic diversity and expanding or improving natural ecosystems. Sustainable Use and Management of Biodiversity Participants explore international targets concerning sustainable biodiversity use and management, together with examples of regional, national and local policies. The course also examines international commitments concerning the sustainable use, harvesting and trade of wild species and their relationship with the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES) . Benefit-Sharing and Traditional Indigenous Knowledge Learners explore international targets concerning access and benefit-sharing. The module introduces important international instruments including: The Nagoya Protocol; The International Treaty on Plant Genetic Resources for Food and Agriculture; and The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. It also considers the importance of protecting traditional knowledge. Biodiversity Finance and Capacity-Building Another module addresses the resources necessary to implement international biodiversity commitments, including: Financial resources; Capacity-building; Technical cooperation; Scientific cooperation; and Access to and transfer of technology. The course concludes with a live closing session and provides learners with insights into potential career paths related to the Global Biodiversity Framework, sustainable development and law. Learners are also invited to join a course alumni network. 3. Key Essentials: The Paris Agreement, Sustainable Development and the Law Climate change is another central focus of the Fall 2026 DE-GSJ programme. The Key Essentials: The Paris Agreement, Sustainable Development and the Law course introduces learners to the Paris Agreement under the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) . The programme connects climate change with wider social, economic, environmental and human rights challenges and examines the role of law in responding to climate impacts and implementing international commitments. It is intended for leaders and learners working in law, policymaking, analysis, practice and reporting across governments, academia, civil society and practitioner communities. Learning Objectives The course seeks to help learners: Understand pressing climate change law and governance challenges; Explore the Paris Agreement; Understand tools available to policymakers and lawmakers, including climate finance, transparency and science; Identify innovative domestic policy and legal solutions; Strengthen the role of law and policy in monitoring and reporting; and Build knowledge relevant to international careers in sustainability and justice. What Will Participants Learn About the Paris Agreement? Course Introduction and Orientation Participants first become familiar with the course structure, resources, instructors and other learners. They are also introduced to the major elements, structures and principles of the Paris Agreement under the UNFCCC . Climate Mitigation and Net-Zero Transitions Learners examine mitigation obligations under the UNFCCC and Paris Agreement, including legal commitments relating to the transition towards net zero. The module examines law and policy measures designed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and efforts to limit average global warming. Climate Adaptation, Resilience and Loss and Damage Participants explore: Adaptation commitments under the Paris Agreement; Nationally Determined Contributions; National adaptation plans; Climate resilience; Legal and governance dimensions of adaptation; and Loss and Damage provisions and related international developments. Climate Finance and Carbon Markets Another module examines climate finance provisions under the Paris Agreement and international efforts to align financial flows with its goals. Learners are also introduced to carbon-market policy structures and low-greenhouse-gas development pathways. Climate Compliance, Capacity and Transparency Participants examine the Paris Agreement s enhanced transparency framework and the modalities, procedures and guidelines developed through subsequent Conferences of the Parties. The course also introduces the functions and objectives of the Paris Agreement Implementation and Compliance Committee (PAICC) . The final module includes a live closing session where instructors provide insights into climate law, governance and possible career pathways. Participants are also invited to join an alumni network. Course Format and Learning Experience The DE-GSJ courses are designed to combine expert instruction with flexible independent learning. According to the programme information provided, courses generally involve approximately eight to ten hours of total learning time , with focused modules delivered by University of Cambridge and international experts. The learning experience can include: Recorded or focused expert instruction; Live classroom engagements; Access to selected learning materials; Independent reading; Recommended resources; Self-paced study; Assessments; and Opportunities to engage with instructors and an international community of learners. For example, the programme describes one of its short courses as providing approximately eight hours of learning across six recorded modules, two live Zoom classroom engagements and approximately two to three hours of independent work. This structure makes the programme particularly relevant to professionals and learners who want intensive training without enrolling in a conventional full-time academic degree. Are the DE-GSJ Courses Free? Yes. The programme is designed to widen access to high-quality education, particularly for learners and professionals in countries that are highly vulnerable to climate and sustainability challenges. Successful applicants can undertake the course without paying the normal course value . Each selected learner effectively receives a bursary allowing them to complete the training at no charge. The programme information states that the course is valued at £800 . Importantly, this does not mean that successful participants receive £800 as a cash payment. Instead, the bursary covers access to the educational opportunity, meaning the selected learner does not have to pay the £800 course value. What Do Successful Learners Receive? The DE-GSJ initiative is a non-credit-bearing programme . This distinction is important for applicants who may otherwise assume that completing a course provides academic credits toward a University of Cambridge degree. However, successful completion offers other valuable professional-development benefits. Upon successfully completing each course, learners are eligible to receive a certificate from leading expert institutes of the University of Cambridge and global partners . Successful completion may also provide access to potential further scholarship opportunities for intensive professional development courses through Cambridge Advance Online . For professionals working in government, law, policy, international development, climate change, sustainability, human rights or civil society, the combination of specialised knowledge, certification and access to an international learning network can provide a useful foundation for continued professional development. Who Can Participate? The DE-GSJ Programme is primarily designed to train law and policy leaders . However, participation is not described as being exclusively restricted to lawyers or policymakers. Individuals who are committed to making a difference through law and policy in support of sustainable development may also seek to become part of the programme s wider community of practice. The individual courses specifically reference leaders and learners involved in: Government; Law; Policymaking; Policy analysis; Legal practice; Policy practice; Reporting and monitoring; Academia; Civil society; and Practitioner communities. This makes the opportunity potentially relevant to professionals and emerging leaders whose work intersects with sustainable development, environmental governance, climate action, biodiversity, international development or public policy. Is the Programme Available Internationally? Yes. The DE-GSJ Programme describes its mission in global terms and states that it provides free and accessible sustainability law and policy courses to learners from around the world , with particular emphasis on strengthening capacity in highly vulnerable countries. The supplied programme information does not state a restriction limiting the Fall 2026 courses to one nationality, race or continent. Applicants should nevertheless carefully review the application form and individual course requirements before applying. Language of Instruction The courses are currently offered only in English . Prospective participants should therefore consider whether they have sufficient English-language ability to follow expert instruction, complete readings and other independent learning activities, participate in live engagements and successfully complete required assessments. Certificates and Alumni Network Successful course completion can provide more than knowledge of a particular international agreement. Participants may become eligible for a certificate associated with leading University of Cambridge expert institutes and global partners. Individual courses also indicate that learners can be invited to become part of a course alumni network following completion. For example, both the biodiversity and Paris Agreement course descriptions reference invitations to join a network of course alumni. Such networks can help participants remain connected to a broader international community interested in sustainability, justice, international law and policy. How to Apply for the DE-GSJ Fall Courses 2026 The application process begins through the programme s Educational Offerings section. Applicants should follow these general steps: Review the available courses. Read the course descriptions and identify the Fall 2026 offering or offerings most relevant to your professional interests and development goals. Submit an Expression of Interest. Use the Expression of Interest form provided through the DE-GSJ Educational Offerings page. Check your email. After submitting the Expression of Interest form, prospective learners should receive further information and detailed instructions for completing the full application. Submit a separate application where required. Applicants interested in more than one course should follow the programme s instructions for submitting the necessary application for each course. Submit before the deadline. The programme states that applicants seeking consideration for the Fall Courses must submit their application by 1 September 2026 at 11:59 PM BST . Wait for the selection decision. Applications are reviewed by the programme s selection committee, and applicants are notified by email regarding whether they have been selected. Because participation is free for successful applicants, prospective learners should provide accurate and thoughtful information demonstrating their interest in the programme and their commitment to applying law and policy knowledge toward sustainable development. APPLY NOW Application Deadline The deadline for full applications to the DE-GSJ Fall Courses 2026 is: 1 September 2026 at 11:59 PM BST. Prospective applicants should avoid waiting until the deadline because the process begins with an Expression of Interest, after which additional application instructions are sent by email. The programme provides an unusual opportunity to access specialised international sustainability law and policy education without paying the stated £800 course value. Potential advantages include: Free participation for successful applicants; Learning from University of Cambridge and global experts; Specialised training in sustainability law and governance; Flexible online and self-paced learning; Live classroom engagement; Exposure to an international community of learners; Training relating to major international treaties and frameworks; A certificate following successful completion; Access to an alumni network through relevant courses; Potential access to further scholarship opportunities for professional development through Cambridge Advance Online; and Knowledge that can potentially be applied in government, policy, law, academia, civil society and sustainability-related professional settings. The programme can be especially relevant for individuals seeking to connect global commitments such as the Sustainable Development Goals, Convention on Biological Diversity and Paris Agreement with practical legal and policy implementation. Conclusion The Democratising Education for Global Sustainability and Justice (DE-GSJ) Fall Courses 2026 provide an accessible pathway for professionals, emerging leaders and committed learners around the world to deepen their understanding of sustainability through the lens of international law and public policy. Co-hosted by Lucy Cavendish College and Hughes Hall at the University of Cambridge , the programme is particularly focused on building the capacity of law and policy specialists and empowering communities and governments, including those in highly vulnerable countries, to respond to interconnected global challenges. With Fall 2026 courses covering the Sustainable Development Goals, Convention on Biological Diversity and Paris Agreement , participants can engage with some of the most consequential international frameworks shaping sustainable development, biodiversity protection and global climate action. Successful applicants receive access to the training without paying the stated £800 course value, while successful completion can lead to certification, connections with an international alumni community and potential further professional-development scholarship opportunities.
